artists.name: Michelangelo
artists.bio: Michelangelo Buonarroti trained briefly in Domenico Ghirlandaio's Florentine workshop and studied ancient sculpture in the household of Lorenzo de' Medici. He thought of himself first as a sculptor, and carved the Pietà and David before he was thirty. He painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling, returned decades later for The Last Judgment on its altar wall, and at 71 became architect of St Peter's. He was the first Western artist whose biography was published in his lifetime.

artists.name: Jacques-Louis David
artists.bio: Jacques-Louis David trained in Paris under Joseph-Marie Vien and won the Prix de Rome in 1774 after several failed attempts. His Oath of the Horatii traded Rococo charm for stern classical virtue and clear, sculptural drawing. A revolutionary deputy, he voted for the execution of Louis XVI, painted The Death of Marat, was jailed after Robespierre fell, then became Napoleon's painter. His pupils, among them Ingres and Gros, shaped French painting for a generation, though he died in exile in Brussels.

artists.name: Ilya Repin
artists.bio: Ilya Repin was born in Chuhuiv in Ukraine, painted icons as a teenager and studied at the Imperial Academy of Arts in Saint Petersburg. Barge Haulers on the Volga made his name in 1873, and he became the leading painter among the Peredvizhniki realists. His Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan was pulled from exhibition in 1885. He also painted searching portraits of Tolstoy and Mussorgsky, and died at his house in Kuokkala, which had become part of Finland after the revolution.

artists.name: Grant Wood
artists.bio: Grant Wood grew up in Iowa, trained at the Minneapolis Handicraft Guild and the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, and made several study trips to Europe. Seeing Early Netherlandish painting in Munich in 1928 pushed him toward a crisp, polished realism. American Gothic, shown in Chicago in 1930, made him the leading figure of Regionalism alongside Thomas Hart Benton and John Steuart Curry. The farmer and his daughter were modelled by Wood's dentist and his sister Nan.

artists.name: Thutmose
artists.bio: Thutmose was court sculptor to the pharaoh Akhenaten, working at the new capital of Akhetaten, modern Amarna, around 1350 BCE. He is known because in 1912 German excavators found his house and workshop, identified by an ivory horse blinker inscribed with his name and title. The studio held the painted bust of Nefertiti, apparently a model for other sculptors to copy, and plaster studies of royal and ordinary faces. They show the closely observed naturalism of Amarna art at its best.

artists.name: Gian Lorenzo Bernini
artists.bio: Gian Lorenzo Bernini was born in Naples and trained in Rome under his father, the sculptor Pietro Bernini. In his twenties he carved Apollo and Daphne and David for Cardinal Scipione Borghese, turning marble into flesh, leaves and hair in mid-motion. He served a succession of popes, designing the baldacchino and colonnade of St Peter's and the Fountain of the Four Rivers. In the Ecstasy of Saint Teresa he fused sculpture, architecture and hidden light into a single theatre.

artists.name: Myron
artists.bio: Myron came from Eleutherae, on the border of Attica and Boeotia, and was a leading Athenian sculptor of the mid-5th century BCE; Pliny says he trained under Ageladas of Argos. He worked almost only in bronze and was famed for athletes caught in bold, complex poses. None of his originals survive: his Discobolus, frozen at the top of its swing, is known from Roman marble copies. Ancient writers praised a bronze heifer by him so lifelike that it inspired dozens of epigrams.

artists.name: Thomas Gainsborough
artists.bio: Thomas Gainsborough, son of a Sudbury wool manufacturer, went to London at thirteen and learned from the French engraver Hubert Gravelot. He made his living with portraits, first in Ipswich and Bath and then in London, painted in a light palette with quick, feathery strokes. Landscapes were what he loved most, and he is credited with Richard Wilson as a founder of the British landscape school. He was a founding member of the Royal Academy and the great rival of Joshua Reynolds.

artists.name: Giorgione
artists.bio: Giorgio da Castelfranco, called Giorgione, probably trained in Venice under Giovanni Bellini and died there in 1510, still in his thirties, reportedly of plague. Only about six paintings are firmly his, yet with the young Titian he set Venetian painting on its course of soft colour, atmosphere and mood. The meaning of his subjects, above all The Tempest, has never been settled. Titian finished some of his pictures, one reason attributions between the two remain disputed.

artists.name: Ivan Aivazovsky
artists.bio: Ivan Aivazovsky was born to an Armenian family in the Crimean port of Feodosia and trained at the Imperial Academy of Arts in Saint Petersburg. Appointed painter to the Russian Navy, he spent almost sixty years painting the sea, mostly in the studio and from memory, and produced about 6,000 works. His storms, shipwrecks and moonlit bays, with their glowing, translucent light, made him famous across Europe. Chekhov helped make "worthy of Aivazovsky's brush" a Russian byword for beauty.

artists.name: Eadfrith of Lindisfarne
artists.bio: Eadfrith was bishop of Lindisfarne, the island monastery off the Northumbrian coast, probably from 698 until his death in 721. A note added to the Lindisfarne Gospels in the 10th century names him as its scribe and artist, making him one of the few named makers of early medieval art. The book appears to be the work of a single hand, blending Celtic knotwork, Anglo-Saxon animal ornament and Mediterranean figures. Some historians think he commissioned it rather than made it himself.

artists.name: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
artists.bio: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres, from Montauban, trained in Paris under Jacques-Louis David and won the Prix de Rome in 1801. He spent eighteen years in Rome and Florence, where Paris critics called his work bizarre and archaic, and he supported himself with pencil portraits of visitors. He wanted to be a history painter, but his portraits and nudes, with their pure contours and deliberate distortions, are his lasting achievement. Matisse and Picasso both learned from him.

artists.name: Andrea Mantegna
artists.bio: Andrea Mantegna, a carpenter's son, was apprenticed at eleven to the Paduan painter and collector of antiquities Francesco Squarcione. He brought an archaeologist's eye to painting: figures as hard as carved stone, accurate Roman architecture and daring foreshortening. From 1460 he was court painter to the Gonzaga in Mantua, where he frescoed the Camera degli Sposi with its painted oculus open to the sky. He married Jacopo Bellini's daughter, making Giovanni Bellini his brother-in-law.

artists.name: Paolo Veronese
artists.bio: Paolo Caliari took his nickname from Verona, where he trained, and settled in Venice in the 1550s. With Titian and Tintoretto he dominated Venetian painting, known for luminous colour, silvery light and vast banquets set in marble architecture, such as The Wedding at Cana. In 1573 the Inquisition questioned him over the dogs, dwarfs and German soldiers in his Last Supper. Rather than change the picture, he renamed it The Feast in the House of Levi.

artists.name: James McNeill Whistler
artists.bio: James McNeill Whistler was born in Massachusetts, spent part of his boyhood in Saint Petersburg and left West Point before settling in Paris and then London. A leading voice of "art for art's sake", he gave his paintings musical titles, arrangements, harmonies and nocturnes, to put tone and colour ahead of story. When John Ruskin accused him of flinging a pot of paint in the public's face, Whistler sued for libel in 1878 and won a farthing in damages.

artists.name: Donatello
artists.bio: Donatello trained in Florence as a goldsmith and worked in Lorenzo Ghiberti's workshop before studying ancient ruins in Rome, reportedly alongside Brunelleschi. He moved Florentine sculpture from Gothic grace to classical weight and raw feeling, and developed rilievo schiacciato, a very shallow carved relief. His bronze David, made for the Medici, was the first freestanding male nude since antiquity. In Padua he cast the Gattamelata, the first large bronze equestrian statue since Roman times.

artists.name: Ivan Shishkin
artists.bio: Ivan Shishkin, a merchant's son from Yelabuga, studied at the Moscow School of Painting and the Imperial Academy of Arts in Saint Petersburg, then in Germany and Switzerland. A founding member of the Peredvizhniki, he painted Russian forests with an almost botanical exactness, tree by tree and needle by needle. He was also a fine etcher and draughtsman. His best-known picture, Morning in a Pine Forest, is a joint work: the bears were painted by Konstantin Savitsky.

artists.name: Andrea del Verrocchio
artists.bio: Andrea del Verrocchio trained as a goldsmith and ran one of the busiest workshops in Florence, producing sculpture, paintings and metalwork, much of it for the Medici. His pupils included Leonardo da Vinci, Perugino and Lorenzo di Credi, and Leonardo painted one of the angels in his Baptism of Christ. As a sculptor he made a bronze David and Christ and Saint Thomas. His equestrian statue of Bartolomeo Colleoni in Venice was cast after his death.

artists.name: John Constable
artists.bio: John Constable, a corn merchant's son from East Bergholt in Suffolk, trained at the Royal Academy Schools and devoted himself to the countryside of the Stour valley around his home. He made open-air oil sketches and cloud studies, catching weather and light with flecks of white paint. The Hay Wain won a gold medal at the Paris Salon of 1824 and impressed French painters, yet he sold little in England and became a full Academician only at 52.

artists.name: El Greco
artists.bio: Doménikos Theotokópoulos trained as an icon painter in Venetian-ruled Crete, then studied Titian and Tintoretto in Venice and worked in Rome. In 1577 he settled in Toledo, where he stayed for the rest of his life, still signing his pictures in Greek letters and often adding "Cretan". His elongated figures, flickering light and acid colour puzzled many contemporaries. Rediscovered around 1900, he was hailed as a forerunner of both Expressionism and Cubism.

artists.name: Joseph Wright of Derby
artists.bio: Joseph Wright, a lawyer's son from Derby, trained in London under the portraitist Thomas Hudson and spent most of his career in his home town. He is best known for candlelit scenes of science, such as A Philosopher Lecturing on the Orrery and An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump, where one hidden light picks out rapt faces. His links to the Lunar Society's scientists and industrialists made him the first painter of the Industrial Revolution, from forges to cotton mills.

artists.name: Polykleitos
artists.bio: Polykleitos of Argos was one of the most admired sculptors of 5th-century BCE Greece, working mainly in bronze. In a treatise called the Canon he set out a system of ideal proportions for the male body, and his Doryphoros, or Spear-Bearer, was taken as its model. The figure's weight rests on one leg, with hips and shoulders tilted in answer, a pattern classical sculpture followed for centuries. No originals survive; his work is known through Roman marble copies.

artists.name: Rogier van der Weyden
artists.bio: Rogier van der Weyden, born Roger de la Pasture in Tournai, probably trained under Robert Campin before becoming official painter to the city of Brussels in 1436. His Descent from the Cross shows grief with new intensity, the figures pressed into a shallow space like painted sculpture. He worked for Philip the Good and the Burgundian nobility, and his paintings were exported to Italy and Spain. Widely copied, he is often called the most influential Northern painter of the 15th century.

artists.name: Ivan Kramskoi
artists.bio: Ivan Kramskoi came from a poor family in Ostrogozhsk and studied at the Imperial Academy of Arts in Saint Petersburg, where in 1863 he led the "Revolt of the Fourteen", graduates who refused the set subject and walked out. He co-founded the Peredvizhniki and became its chief spokesman, arguing that art had a public and moral duty. He is best known for Christ in the Desert, the enigmatic Unknown Woman, and portraits of Tolstoy and other leading Russians.

artists.name: Henri Rousseau
artists.bio: Henri Rousseau collected tolls on goods entering Paris, which earned him the nickname Le Douanier, and taught himself to paint, only working full-time from his late forties. Critics mocked the flat, meticulous pictures he showed at the Salon des Indépendants, but younger artists admired them, and Picasso held a banquet in his honour in 1908. His famous jungles came from visits to the Paris botanical garden and zoo, not from travel: he never left France.

artists.name: Karl Bryullov
artists.bio: Karl Bryullov, son of a woodcarver of Huguenot descent, trained at the Imperial Academy of Arts in Saint Petersburg and left for Italy in 1822. In Rome he painted The Last Day of Pompeii, a vast scene of Vesuvius erupting that caused a sensation in Italy before its triumphant arrival in Russia. Back in Saint Petersburg he taught at the Academy and painted brilliant society portraits. He was one of the first Russian painters to win a European reputation.

artists.name: Zhang Zeduan
artists.bio: Almost everything known about Zhang Zeduan comes from a colophon of 1186 on his handscroll Along the River During the Qingming Festival. It says he came from Dongwu in Shandong, studied in the Northern Song capital, Kaifeng, and specialised in precise ruled-line painting of boats, carts, markets and bridges. The scroll, over five metres long, follows crowds of people from the countryside through the city gate. His birth and death dates are only traditional estimates.

artists.name: Petrus Christus
artists.bio: Petrus Christus was born in Baarle and became a citizen of Bruges in 1444, three years after Jan van Eyck's death. Until Hans Memling arrived he was the city's leading painter, working in a precise manner indebted to Van Eyck and Rogier van der Weyden. He was among the first Northern painters to build a picture on a single vanishing point, and he set sitters in real rooms rather than against flat backgrounds, as in his Portrait of a Carthusian.

artists.name: Praxiteles
artists.bio: Praxiteles, son of the sculptor Cephisodotus the Elder, was the most celebrated Athenian sculptor of the 4th century BCE. His Aphrodite of Knidos was the first life-size statue of a fully nude woman in Greek art, and it drew visitors to Knidos for centuries. He gave gods relaxed, S-curved poses and soft, polished surfaces. No surviving statue is certainly by his hand, and whether the Hermes with the Infant Dionysus at Olympia is an original is still argued over.

artists.name: Frederic Leighton
artists.bio: Frederic Leighton, son of a wealthy Scarborough doctor, trained on the Continent, in Frankfurt, Florence and Rome, before settling in London. He painted classical and biblical subjects with a polished academic finish and luxuriant colour, most famously Flaming June, and was also a sculptor. He became President of the Royal Academy in 1878. Made a baron in January 1896, he died the next day, giving him the shortest-lived peerage in British history.

artists.name: Parmigianino
artists.bio: Francesco Mazzola, called Parmigianino, "the little one from Parma", trained with his painter uncles and was working in Parma churches in his teens. His Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror helped win him a welcome in Rome in 1524; Vasari says soldiers sacking the city in 1527 found him at his easel and spared him. His elongated, elegant figures, as in the unfinished Madonna with the Long Neck, define early Mannerism. He was also among the first Italian painters to make etchings himself.

artists.name: Emanuel Leutze
artists.bio: Emanuel Leutze was born in Württemberg and grew up in Philadelphia, where he painted portraits as a teenager to support his family. In 1840 he returned to Germany to study at the Düsseldorf academy and stayed nearly twenty years, helping many visiting American artists. There he painted Washington Crossing the Delaware (1851), hoping to encourage Europe's liberal reformers after the failed revolutions of 1848. Back in America he painted the mural Westward the Course of Empire Takes Its Way in the Capitol.

artists.name: Hans Memling
artists.bio: Hans Memling was born in Seligenstadt near Frankfurt and probably worked in Rogier van der Weyden's Brussels workshop before becoming a citizen of Bruges in 1465. There he ran a large workshop, and a tax list of 1480 places him among the city's wealthiest residents. His calm, finely balanced altarpieces and portraits drew Italian merchants as well as local patrons. His Last Judgment, bound for Florence, was seized at sea by a Danzig privateer in 1473 and is still in Gdańsk.

artists.name: Peter Paul Rubens
artists.bio: Peter Paul Rubens was born in Siegen in Germany to exiles from Antwerp and trained in Antwerp before spending eight years in Italy studying Titian, Michelangelo and ancient sculpture. Back home he ran a large workshop that produced altarpieces, myths, hunts and portraits for courts across Europe, full of movement, colour and flesh. He was also a diplomat, knighted by Philip IV of Spain and by Charles I of England, for whom he painted the Banqueting House ceiling in Whitehall.

artists.name: William-Adolphe Bouguereau
artists.bio: William-Adolphe Bouguereau trained at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris and won the Prix de Rome in 1850. He painted nymphs, mythologies and idealised peasant girls with flawless anatomy and a porcelain finish, and became the model Salon painter of his generation, honoured and highly paid in France and America. The Impressionists despised him, and his reputation collapsed after his death until a revival in the 1980s. In 1896 he married his former student, the American painter Elizabeth Jane Gardner.

artists.name: Bronzino
artists.bio: Agnolo di Cosimo, called Bronzino, was the son of a Florentine butcher and trained under Pontormo, who is thought to have painted him as a boy in one of his Joseph panels. From his late thirties he was court painter to Cosimo I de' Medici, producing cool, polished portraits of sitters who give nothing away. His Venus, Cupid, Folly and Time is a knot of eroticism and learned allegory. He also wrote poetry, both serious and comic.

artists.name: Lysippos
artists.bio: Lysippos of Sicyon began as a bronze worker, largely taught himself sculpture and rose to head the school of Argos and Sicyon. He replaced the sturdy proportions of Polykleitos with leaner bodies and smaller heads, making figures seem taller and more alive in space, as in the Apoxyomenos. Pliny credits him with some 1,500 bronzes, none known to survive in the original. Alexander the Great reportedly allowed no other sculptor to portray him.

artists.name: Matthias Grünewald
artists.bio: Mathis Gothart Nithart, known since the 17th century by the mistaken name Grünewald, served as court artist to the archbishops of Mainz and also worked as a hydraulic engineer. He turned away from the classical harmony of his contemporary Dürer and painted with late Gothic intensity and blazing colour. His Isenheim Altarpiece, made for a monastery that nursed victims of ergotism and plague, shows Christ's body torn and pitted with sores. Only ten paintings and some 35 drawings survive.

artists.name: Henry Fuseli
artists.bio: Johann Heinrich Füssli was trained for the Zurich church and took holy orders, but helping to expose a corrupt magistrate forced him to leave Switzerland. In London Joshua Reynolds urged him to paint, and eight years in Rome studying Michelangelo gave him his taut, straining figures. He specialised in the supernatural and the extreme, and The Nightmare (1781) made him famous. He became Professor of Painting at the Royal Academy and influenced the young William Blake.

artists.name: Albrecht Altdorfer
artists.bio: Albrecht Altdorfer spent his career in Regensburg, where he was also town architect and a councillor. A journey along the Danube into the Alps around 1511 turned him toward landscape, and as the leading painter of the Danube School he made forests and mountains the real subject of his pictures, painting some of the first pure landscapes in European art. His Battle of Alexander at Issus (1529), made for Duke William IV of Bavaria, sets a vast battle beneath a cosmic sky.

artists.name: Piero della Francesca
artists.bio: Piero della Francesca grew up in Sansepolcro, worked in Florence with Domenico Veneziano and absorbed the lessons of Masaccio and Brunelleschi. His pictures are built from clear geometry and pale, even daylight, with still, monumental figures that rarely show emotion. His fresco cycle of the Legend of the True Cross in San Francesco, Arezzo, is his largest work. He was also a serious mathematician who wrote treatises on perspective and geometry.

artists.name: Tintoretto
artists.bio: Jacopo Robusti was nicknamed Tintoretto, "little dyer", after his father's trade. He is said to have lasted only days in Titian's studio and was largely self-taught, aiming, according to an early biographer, for the drawing of Michelangelo and the colour of Titian. His speed and daring earned him the name il Furioso: steep perspectives, flickering light and muscular figures in violent motion. He spent more than two decades decorating the Scuola Grande di San Rocco in Venice.

artists.name: Giovanni Bellini
artists.bio: Giovanni Bellini grew up in the household of Jacopo Bellini, at the centre of Venice's leading family of painters, and Andrea Mantegna became his brother-in-law. Moving from tempera to oil, he used slow-drying glazes to bathe Madonnas, Pietàs and saints in soft, warm light and luminous landscape. He made Venice a centre of painting to rival Florence and taught both Giorgione and Titian. In his eighties he was still experimenting, painting The Feast of the Gods for Alfonso d'Este in 1514.

artists.name: Apollonius of Tralles
artists.bio: Apollonius and his brother Tauriscus came from Tralles in Asia Minor and worked in the Rhodian tradition of dramatic, many-figured marble groups. Pliny records their group of Zethus and Amphion tying Dirce to a wild bull, carved from a single block, which the Roman collector Asinius Pollio brought from Rhodes. The Farnese Bull in Naples is a Roman version of it. Pliny adds that the brothers named their teacher Menecrates as their father, though their natural father was Artemidorus.

artists.name: Antonio Canova
artists.bio: Antonio Canova, a stonecutter's son from Possagno, learned to carve in his grandfather's workshop and trained in Venice before settling in Rome in 1781. His marbles, from Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss to Pauline Borghese as Venus, gave Neoclassicism its softest, most polished surfaces. He was the most celebrated sculptor in Europe, working for popes and for Napoleon. After Napoleon's fall he went to Paris as papal envoy and recovered many works of art taken from Italy.

artists.name: Lawrence Alma-Tadema
artists.bio: Born in Friesland, Lawrence Alma-Tadema trained at the Antwerp Academy and worked with the history painter Hendrik Leys before settling in London in 1870. He built a lucrative career painting daily life in ancient Rome, Greece and Egypt, with marble that looks cool to the touch and archaeological detail drawn from Pompeii. He was knighted in 1899. He numbered his paintings with Roman numerals as opus numbers, reaching more than 400.

artists.name: Correggio
artists.bio: Antonio Allegri took his name from Correggio, the small Emilian town where he was born, and spent most of his career in Parma. He painted with soft, smoky modelling and warm flesh, and was a master of chiaroscuro. His dome frescoes in Parma, above all the Assumption of the Virgin in the cathedral, send swirls of figures upward in steep foreshortening, a device Baroque ceiling painters later adopted. His Jupiter and Io is among the most sensuous pictures of the Renaissance.

artists.name: Jan Matejko
artists.bio: Jan Matejko entered the Kraków School of Fine Arts at fourteen and studied in Munich and Vienna before returning to Kraków for good. At a time when Poland was partitioned and had no state, he painted its history on a huge scale: Stańczyk, Rejtan, the Union of Lublin and the Battle of Grunwald. Critics called his crowded, theatrical canvases old-fashioned, but for Poles they became a kind of national memory. From 1873 he directed the Kraków school.

artists.name: Arkhip Kuindzhi
artists.bio: Arkhip Kuindzhi, of Greek origin, was orphaned at six and grew up poor around Mariupol and Taganrog before reaching the St Petersburg Academy of Arts. He exhibited with the Peredvizhniki but left them to pursue his own effects of light, painting moonlight, sunsets and storm-light in intense, simplified colour. In 1880 Moonlit Night on the Dnieper was shown alone in a darkened room, and crowds queued to see its glowing moon. He was dismissed from teaching at the Academy in 1897 for supporting student protests.

artists.name: Osman Hamdi Bey
artists.bio: Osman Hamdi Bey, son of a future grand vizier, went to Paris to study law but switched to painting under Jean-Léon Gérôme and Gustave Boulanger. Back in Istanbul he became the Ottoman Empire's first archaeologist and museum director, founding what are now the Istanbul Archaeology Museums and the Academy of Fine Arts. His paintings answer European Orientalism from the inside, with learned, dignified figures in Ottoman settings. His best-known picture is The Tortoise Trainer (1906).

artists.name: Hugo van der Goes
artists.bio: Hugo van der Goes became a master in the Ghent painters' guild in 1467 and later served as its dean. His altarpieces combine monumental figures, rich colour and startlingly individual faces, above all the rough shepherds of the Portinari Triptych, which reached Florence in 1483 and impressed Italian painters. Around 1475 he entered the Rood Klooster near Brussels as a lay brother. There, not long before his death, he suffered a severe mental breakdown.

artists.name: Alexandre Cabanel
artists.bio: Alexandre Cabanel, a carpenter's son from Montpellier, trained at the École des Beaux-Arts and won the Prix de Rome in 1845. He painted history, religious and mythological subjects and fashionable portraits with a smooth, polished finish. His Birth of Venus was bought by Napoleon III at the Salon of 1863, the year Manet's Déjeuner sur l'herbe hung in the Salon des Refusés. As a teacher and Salon juror he shaped French academic painting for decades.

artists.name: Benvenuto Cellini
artists.bio: Benvenuto Cellini trained as a goldsmith in Florence and made his name in Rome working for popes, then served Francis I of France, for whom he made a gold and enamel salt cellar. Back in Florence he cast the bronze Perseus with the Head of Medusa for Cosimo I de' Medici. His autobiography, full of brawls, killings, imprisonment and boasting, is one of the liveliest documents of the Renaissance. In it he claims to have shot the Constable of Bourbon during the Sack of Rome.

artists.name: Jusepe de Ribera
artists.bio: Jusepe de Ribera was born in Xàtiva near Valencia, went to Italy young and settled in Spanish-ruled Naples, where Italians called him Lo Spagnoletto, "the little Spaniard". Following Caravaggio, he painted with hard tenebrist light and unsparing realism: flayed and crucified martyrs, and wrinkled beggars posed as ancient philosophers. His later works grew lighter and richer in colour. Working for the Spanish viceroys, he became the dominant painter in Naples.

artists.name: Jean-Léon Gérôme
artists.bio: Jean-Léon Gérôme studied under Paul Delaroche and made his name at the Salon of 1847 with The Cock Fight. His meticulously finished scenes of ancient Rome and the Middle East, such as Pollice Verso, were reproduced so widely by the firm of his father-in-law, Adolphe Goupil, that by 1880 he was arguably the most famous living artist. He taught at the École des Beaux-Arts for decades, with pupils including Thomas Eakins and Osman Hamdi Bey, and fiercely opposed Impressionism.

artists.name: Amedeo Modigliani
artists.bio: Amedeo Modigliani grew up in a Sephardic Jewish family in Livorno and studied the art of antiquity and the Renaissance before moving to Paris in 1906. From 1909 to 1914 he worked mainly on carved stone heads, in contact with Brâncuși. He then returned to painting: portraits and nudes with long necks, oval, masklike faces and blank almond eyes. Poor and ill for much of his life, he died of tubercular meningitis at 35, and fame came only afterwards.

artists.name: Carel Fabritius
artists.bio: Carel Fabritius first worked as a carpenter, which may explain his Latin surname, and studied with Rembrandt in Amsterdam in the early 1640s. Settling in Delft, he moved away from his master's dark manner, setting figures against pale backgrounds and experimenting with perspective and daylight. He died at 32 in the Delft gunpowder explosion of 1654, which also destroyed most of his work. Only about a dozen paintings survive, among them The Goldfinch.

artists.name: Apollonius of Athens
artists.bio: Apollonius, son of Nestor, an Athenian, carved his name prominently on the base of the Belvedere Torso, but no ancient writer mentions him. He probably worked for Roman patrons in the 1st century BCE, making marble versions of earlier Hellenistic statues. The seated, twisting Torso, known in Rome since the 1430s, was studied closely by Michelangelo and shaped his muscular figure style. The bronze Boxer at Rest in Rome has also been attributed to him, though this is debated.

artists.name: Agasias of Ephesus
artists.bio: Agasias, son of Dositheus, of Ephesus is known only from his signature on the base of the Borghese Gladiator, carved around 100 BCE. The life-size marble shows a nude warrior lunging forward, probably against a mounted opponent, with every muscle strained. Found at Anzio in the early 17th century, it became one of the most admired and copied antique statues in Europe. Whether other signed works by men named Agasias are by the same sculptor is unclear.

artists.name: Duccio
artists.bio: Duccio di Buoninsegna was the leading painter of Siena around 1300. He softened the Byzantine tradition with tender expressions, flowing line and a new sense of space, laying the foundations of the Sienese school. His Maestà for the high altar of Siena Cathedral, completed in 1311, was carried from his workshop to the cathedral in a public procession. City records also show a life troubled by debts and fines.

artists.name: Francesco Melzi
artists.bio: Francesco Melzi came from a noble Milanese family and joined Leonardo da Vinci as a young pupil around 1506. He stayed with Leonardo for the rest of the master's life, following him to Rome and then to France, and painted in close imitation of his style. Leonardo left him his notebooks and drawings, and Melzi compiled from them the Codex Urbinas, the basis of the Treatise on Painting. After his death his heirs let the papers be dispersed.

artists.name: Robert Campin
artists.bio: Robert Campin was the leading painter of Tournai for some thirty years and, with Jan van Eyck, a founder of Early Netherlandish painting. No surviving work is signed or documented as his, but he is now usually identified with the Master of Flémalle, whose panels set sacred scenes in solid, cluttered Flemish rooms. His workshop trained Rogier van der Weyden and Jacques Daret. In 1432 he was prosecuted for an affair with a woman named Laurence Polette.

artists.name: Frans Hals
artists.bio: Frans Hals was born in Antwerp, but his family fled to Haarlem when he was a child, and he lived there for the rest of his life. He studied under Karel van Mander and became the city's leading portraitist, painting civic guards, regents and ordinary citizens. His loose, rapid brushwork catches laughs, glances and shifting poses with a freedom no contemporary matched. Neglected after his death, he was rediscovered in the 19th century by painters including Manet.

artists.name: Simone Martini
artists.bio: Simone Martini probably trained in the circle of Duccio in Siena, where he painted the Maestà fresco in the Palazzo Pubblico in 1315. His art, with its sinuous line, gold and courtly elegance, drew on French manuscripts and ivories and helped shape the International Gothic style. With his brother-in-law Lippo Memmi he painted the Annunciation of 1333, now in the Uffizi. He spent his last years at the papal court in Avignon, where he befriended the poet Petrarch.

artists.name: Huang Gongwang
artists.bio: Huang Gongwang was born Lu Jian in Changshu and later adopted into the Huang family. After a minor official career under the Mongol Yuan dynasty ended in prison, he turned to Daoism and painting, becoming the eldest of the Four Masters of the Yuan. He built mountains from dry, layered brushstrokes and pale ink washes, in the scholar's manner rather than the court academy's. His handscroll Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains, painted around the age of eighty, became a model for centuries of Chinese landscape painters.

artists.name: Han Gan
artists.bio: Han Gan came from a poor family and, according to tradition, was noticed as a young man by the poet Wang Wei, who helped him study painting. He trained under the court painter Cao Ba and served at the Tang court under Emperor Xuanzong. He painted Buddhist and Daoist figures, but was famed above all for horses, said to have learned from the animals in the imperial stables rather than from earlier paintings. Night-Shining White, a portrait of the emperor's charger, is attributed to him.

artists.name: Yan Liben
artists.bio: Yan Liben came from an aristocratic family of painters and officials; his father and elder brother both worked as artists at court. He painted portraits for Emperor Taizong, including the meritorious officials of the Lingyan Pavilion, and rose through government to serve as chancellor under Emperor Gaozong. He also worked as an architect. The Thirteen Emperors Scroll in Boston, with its procession of rulers from the Han to the Sui, is the one surviving work widely accepted as partly his.

artists.name: Fan Kuan
artists.bio: Fan Kuan, whose given name was Fan Zhongzheng, lived as a recluse in the mountains of Shaanxi in the early Northern Song. He is said to have given up copying earlier masters in order to learn directly from nature. His towering hanging scroll Travellers among Mountains and Streams, perhaps his only surviving work, set the ideal of monumental landscape: a vast cliff face above a tiny mule train. His signature, hidden among the foliage, was only rediscovered in 1958.

artists.name: Tawaraya Sōtatsu
artists.bio: Tawaraya Sōtatsu ran a painting workshop in Kyoto that made fans and decorated papers, and collaborated for years with the calligrapher Hon'ami Kōetsu, painting gold and silver designs beneath his poems. He popularised tarashikomi, dropping wet pigment into still-wet paint to create pooled, mottled effects. His folding screens, above all Wind God and Thunder God, set bold, simplified forms against bare gold grounds. With Kōetsu he is regarded as the founder of the Rinpa school, later continued by Ogata Kōrin.

artists.name: Limbourg brothers
artists.bio: Herman, Paul and Johan Limbourg were nephews of the painter Jean Malouel, trained as goldsmiths and became the finest manuscript illuminators of their day. Working for Jean, Duke of Berry, they filled books of hours with minutely observed landscapes, castles and courtly life. All three died in 1416, probably of plague, leaving the Très Riches Heures unfinished; Jean Colombe completed it about seventy years later.

artists.name: Unknown artist, Insular Britain and Ireland

artworks.title: Mona Lisa
artworks.blurb: Leonardo's half-length portrait is traditionally identified as Lisa del Giocondo, wife of a Florentine silk merchant, though the sitter is still debated. She sits upright with folded hands before an imagined landscape of winding paths, a bridge and icy mountains. Leonardo built her face without outlines, blending tones in soft sfumato so that the corners of the mouth and eyes stay ambiguous.
artworks.lookCloser: Leonardo set the horizon level with her eyes, tying figure to landscape. She has no visible eyebrows or eyelashes; high-resolution scans suggest they faded or were cleaned away.

artworks.title: Code of Hammurabi
artworks.blurb: This basalt stele carries the longest and best-preserved law collection from the ancient Near East, issued by Hammurabi, sixth king of the First Dynasty of Babylon. About 4,130 lines of cuneiform set out the laws as "if… then" cases covering crime, family, property and trade. Carried off to Susa in Iran as plunder, it was excavated there in 1901–02.
artworks.lookCloser: At the top, the king stands before the enthroned sun god Shamash, god of justice. Near the bottom, seven columns of laws were polished away in antiquity.

artworks.title: Terracotta Army
artworks.collection: Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor, Xi'an
artworks.blurb: More than 8,000 life-size clay soldiers, with chariots and horses, were buried in pits east of the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, China's first emperor, to guard him after his death. Farmers digging a well found them in 1974. Rank is marked by height, armour and hairstyle, and each face was individualised from about ten basic forms.
artworks.lookCloser: The figures were once painted with pigments such as cinnabar, malachite and azurite. Most of the colour flakes within minutes of exposure to air, leaving the grey clay we see now.

artworks.title: The Last Supper
artworks.medium: Tempera on gesso, pitch and mastic
artworks.blurb: Painted for Ludovico Sforza on the end wall of a Milanese convent refectory, the mural shows the moment after Christ announces that one of the apostles will betray him. The twelve react in four groups of three, with shock, anger and disbelief. Leonardo chose tempera over fresco so he could work slowly, and the paint soon began to fail; little original surface survives.
artworks.lookCloser: Judas, leaning back into shadow, clutches a small bag and tips over the salt cellar. Every perspective line in the room converges on Christ's head.

artworks.title: Great Sphinx of Giza
artworks.blurb: Carved from the living rock of the Giza plateau, the Sphinx joins a lion's body to a king's head in the striped nemes headcloth. It is the oldest known monumental sculpture in Egypt, made in the Old Kingdom under Khufu or his son Khafre. No contemporary inscription names it, and whose face it bears is still disputed.
artworks.lookCloser: Between the paws stands the Dream Stele of Thutmose IV, who cleared the sand around 1400 BCE. The nose was prised off with rods or chisels, not shot away by Napoleon's troops.

artworks.title: David
artworks.blurb: Michelangelo carved the biblical giant-killer from a block that other sculptors had begun and abandoned decades earlier. Meant for the roofline of Florence Cathedral, the colossal nude was instead set before the Palazzo della Signoria in 1504, where it stood for the republic's defiance of stronger rivals and the Medici. It was the first colossal marble statue since antiquity.
artworks.lookCloser: David is shown before the fight, sling over his shoulder, weight on one leg. Marks from stones thrown at the statue during its move in 1504 are still visible on his upper back.

artworks.title: Venus de Milo
artworks.blurb: Found by a farmer on the Aegean island of Milos in 1820, this over-life-size marble most likely shows Aphrodite, bare to the hips, with drapery slipping around her legs. It pairs a calm, classical head with the twisting pose and deep-cut folds of Hellenistic sculpture. A now-lost inscription linked it to Alexandros of Antioch, but that attribution is disputed.
artworks.lookCloser: A filled hole below the right breast once held a metal tenon supporting the missing right arm. A marble hand holding an apple, found with the statue, is now thought to belong to it.

artworks.title: Vitruvian Man
artworks.medium: Pen and ink with wash over metalpoint on paper
artworks.blurb: Leonardo tested the Roman architect Vitruvius's claim that a well-made body fits both a circle and a square. One nude man takes two poses at once: arms level inside the square, arms and legs spread inside the circle. Leonardo made the scheme work by centring the circle on the navel and the square on the genitals.
artworks.lookCloser: Tiny tick marks along the arms and legs record Leonardo's measurements, made with compass and ruler. The notes above and below the figure are in his mirror writing.

artworks.title: Venus of Willendorf
artworks.medium: Oolitic limestone with traces of red ochre
artworks.blurb: This palm-sized figure of a nude woman was dug up in 1908 at a Palaeolithic site near Willendorf in Lower Austria. Breasts, belly and hips are full and rounded, thin arms rest on the breasts, and the head has no face. The name reflects old guesses about a fertility goddess; her purpose is unknown, and some scholars prefer "Woman of Willendorf".
artworks.lookCloser: The head is wrapped in circular bands, read as plaited hair or a woven cap. The stone is not local: it most likely came from near Lake Garda in northern Italy.

artworks.title: Bayeux Tapestry
artworks.blurb: Nearly 70 metres of embroidered linen tell the story of the Norman conquest of England, from the last years of Edward the Confessor to William's victory at Hastings in 1066. Probably commissioned by William's half-brother Bishop Odo and stitched in England soon after, it is technically embroidery, not tapestry. Its 58 scenes record ships, castles, clothing and armour in close detail.
artworks.lookCloser: The opening scene shows King Edward the Confessor enthroned, labelled EDWARD REX, speaking with Harold. Every scene carries a short Latin caption stitched above the action.

artworks.title: The Creation of Adam
artworks.blurb: In the fourth of the Genesis scenes on the Sistine Chapel ceiling, painted for Pope Julius II, God sweeps in wrapped in a billowing cloak and a crowd of figures, reaching toward the reclining Adam. Adam is already formed but still inert, his arm mirroring God's. It is one of nine Genesis episodes on a vault of more than 300 figures.
artworks.lookCloser: The two index fingers never touch: a gap of about 2 cm remains. The figure under God's left arm is often read as Eve, though that identification is debated.

artworks.title: Pietà
artworks.blurb: Mary holds the dead Christ across her lap, her face calm and strikingly young for the mother of a grown man. Made for a French cardinal's funeral chapel in Old St Peter's, the group rises as a pyramid, with Mary's vast drapery disguising how hard it is to cradle an adult body. The wounds are reduced to small marks.
artworks.lookCloser: The sash across Mary's chest carries Michelangelo's signature, the only one on any of his works. Vasari says he added it after hearing the statue credited to another sculptor.

artworks.title: Ishtar Gate
artworks.blurb: Nebuchadnezzar II built this double gate into the inner city of Babylon and dedicated it to the goddess Ishtar. Its walls were faced with bricks glazed deep blue in imitation of lapis lazuli, with rows of moulded dragons and bulls in low relief, animals of the gods Marduk and Adad. The smaller front gate was rebuilt in Berlin from excavated fragments.
artworks.lookCloser: Find the mušḫuššu, Marduk's dragon, with a snake's head, a scaly body and a bird's talons on its hind legs. Brick seams were planned never to cross an animal's eye.

artworks.title: Winged Victory of Samothrace
artworks.medium: Parian marble; ship base of grey marble
artworks.blurb: The goddess Nike alights on the prow of a warship, wings spread, her thin tunic pressed against her body by the wind. Found in 1863 in the sanctuary of the Great Gods on Samothrace, the statue lacks its head and arms. It is a rare Hellenistic original rather than a Roman copy, and has crowned the Louvre's Daru staircase since 1884.
artworks.lookCloser: Only the left wing is ancient marble; the right is a plaster replica made in the 1880s. The palm of her right hand, found on Samothrace in 1950, is shown with the statue.

artworks.title: The Potato Eaters
artworks.blurb: Five peasants share a meal of potatoes under a single oil lamp in a cottage at Nuenen. Van Gogh wanted to show people who had "tilled the earth themselves with these hands they are putting in the dish", and painted them coarse on purpose. The dark, earthy palette comes from the Hague School, and two years later he still called it his best work.
artworks.lookCloser: A girl sits with her back to us at the centre of the table, a device Van Gogh may have taken from Jozef Israëls's A Peasant Family at the Table.

artworks.title: Book of Kells
artworks.medium: Ink and pigments on calf vellum
artworks.blurb: This Latin Gospel book was made around 800 by Columban monks, probably begun on Iona and finished at Kells in Ireland. Its pages fuse Christian imagery with the knots, spirals and interlace of Insular art. This page opens the Gospel of John, "In principio erat verbum", with the letters IN P swollen into panels of snakes, crosses and ornament.
artworks.lookCloser: At the top, a curly-haired figure holds a book inside a flame-like border. Scholars disagree whether he is John the Evangelist or Christ as the Word.

artworks.title: The Origin of the World
artworks.blurb: Courbet cropped a reclining woman's body to belly, thighs and genitals, painted close-up without any mythological excuse. It was made for the private erotic collection of the Ottoman diplomat Khalil Bey and stayed hidden from public view for most of its history. Letters point to the dancer Constance Quéniaux as the model, though Joanna Hiffernan has long been proposed.
artworks.lookCloser: Its last private owner, the psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan, kept it behind a sliding panel on which André Masson painted an allusive, Surrealist version of the same image.

artworks.title: The Death of Socrates
artworks.collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
artworks.blurb: Condemned to drink hemlock, Socrates sits upright on his prison bed and keeps teaching, one hand reaching for the cup, the other raised. Around him his pupils give way to grief; the young man passing the poison turns his face away. Drawing on Plato's Phaedo, David set the calm philosopher against his followers' anguish, and the picture triumphed at the Salon of 1787.
artworks.lookCloser: David signed twice: his full name under Crito, who grips Socrates's thigh, and his initials under the aged Plato, slumped at the foot of the bed.

artworks.title: Laocoön and His Sons
artworks.collection: Museo Pio-Clementino, Vatican Museums, Vatican City
artworks.blurb: The Trojan priest Laocoön and his two sons are crushed and bitten by sea serpents after he warned against the wooden horse. Dug up in Rome in 1506, the group is very likely the one Pliny praised and credited to three Rhodian sculptors: Agesander, Athenodoros and Polydorus. Whether it is an original or a copy of an earlier bronze is still argued.
artworks.lookCloser: Laocoön's knotted brow is so extreme that the physiologist Duchenne called it physically impossible. Pliny said the group was carved from one block; it is actually at least seven pieces.

artworks.title: Narmer Palette
artworks.blurb: Found in the temple of Horus at Hierakonpolis in 1897–98, this shield-shaped ceremonial palette carries one of the earliest images of an Egyptian king. On one face Narmer wears the White Crown of Upper Egypt and raises a mace over a kneeling captive; on the other he wears the Red Crown of Lower Egypt. Conventions Egyptian art kept for millennia are already in place.
artworks.lookCloser: Two serpopards, part serpent and part leopard, entwine their long necks around the round hollow where cosmetics would be ground. At the top, a catfish and a chisel spell Narmer's name.

artworks.title: Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks
artworks.blurb: Cossacks crowd round a table, roaring with laughter as a scribe takes down their insulting reply to the Ottoman sultan Mehmed IV, a legend set in 1676 that may never have happened. Repin spent eleven years on the canvas, advised by the historian Dmytro Yavornytsky, with friends and Saint Petersburg academics posing as Cossacks. Alexander III bought it for 35,000 roubles.
artworks.lookCloser: Repin recorded the years he worked on the picture along the lower edge of the canvas. A second, unfinished version is in the Kharkiv Art Museum.

artworks.title: Luncheon on the Grass
artworks.blurb: A naked woman picnics in a wood with two fully dressed young men and looks straight out at us, while a second woman bathes in the stream behind. Rejected by the Salon jury, it caused a scandal at the 1863 Salon des Refusés. Manet took the poses from a Raphael design engraved by Marcantonio Raimondi and painted modern Parisians at the scale of history painting.
artworks.lookCloser: The woman's discarded clothes, a basket of fruit and a round loaf at lower left form a still life. The bather behind is painted far too large for her distance.

artworks.title: American Gothic
artworks.blurb: A stern farmer holding a pitchfork stands with a woman before a white farmhouse in Eldon, Iowa, whose upper window is a pointed Gothic arch. Grant Wood's sister Nan and his dentist, Byron McKeeby, posed; Wood later said the pair were father and daughter. First read as satire of the rural Midwest, it became a Depression-era image of pioneer endurance.
artworks.lookCloser: The three prongs of the pitchfork repeat in the stitching of the man's overalls and in the Gothic window above. Nan trimmed her apron with rickrack cut from their mother's old dresses.

artworks.title: The Anatomy Lesson of Dr Nicolaes Tulp
artworks.blurb: Dr Nicolaes Tulp, Amsterdam's city anatomist, lifts the muscles of a dead man's forearm while seven surgeons of the guild lean in. The corpse is Aris Kindt, hanged for armed robbery earlier that day. The 26-year-old Rembrandt, newly arrived in Amsterdam, turned a group portrait into a drama, though a real dissection would have begun with the chest, not the arm.
artworks.lookCloser: Top left, the signature reads "Rembrant. f. 1632", perhaps his first use of his first name. The paper one surgeon holds carries a list of the sitters' names.

artworks.title: Wheatfield with Crows
artworks.blurb: Under a stormy blue-black sky, crows scatter over a windswept wheatfield at Auvers-sur-Oise, and a red path edged in green runs into the field. Van Gogh painted it on an elongated double-square canvas around 10 July 1890, weeks before his death, and wrote of expressing sadness and extreme loneliness. It is often called his last painting, but it was not.
artworks.lookCloser: The central path leads nowhere, and the crows' direction of flight is left unclear. In the same letter, Van Gogh also called these fields healthy and fortifying.

artworks.title: Irises
artworks.collection: J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles
artworks.blurb: Van Gogh painted this bed of irises in May 1889, in his first weeks at the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole in Saint-Rémy, working outdoors in its walled garden. The cropped view and broad areas of colour owe much to the Japanese prints he collected. Theo showed it at the Salon des Indépendants that September; in 1987 it set a world auction record.
artworks.lookCloser: A pollen cone from the garden's umbrella pines is stuck in the paint. Many petals now read blue because the red in their original violet has faded.

artworks.title: Capitoline Wolf
artworks.blurb: A tense she-wolf with alert ears and glaring eyes suckles the twins Romulus and Remus, legendary founders of Rome. Long taken for an Etruscan bronze of about 480 BCE, the wolf has been radiocarbon-dated to 1021–1153 CE, and the question remains open. The twins are certainly Renaissance additions, made around the time Pope Sixtus IV moved the wolf to the Capitoline in 1471.
artworks.lookCloser: Wolf and babies are made in completely different styles: she stands stiff and watchful, they are absorbed in feeding. The twins are often credited to Antonio del Pollaiuolo.

artworks.title: Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry
artworks.blurb: Paul, Johan and Herman Limbourg painted this book of hours for Jean, Duke of Berry, brother of Charles V of France, in costly pigments and gold. The brothers and the duke all died in 1416, leaving it unfinished, and Jean Colombe completed it in 1485–89. This page shows the Zodiac Man, a doubled figure whose body parts are each governed by a sign.
artworks.lookCloser: The upper corners carry the duke's arms, gold fleurs-de-lis on blue within a red scalloped border; the lower corners hold interlaced letters. Latin texts link the signs to the four temperaments.

artworks.title: The Oath of the Horatii
artworks.blurb: Three Roman brothers raise their arms to swear on the swords their father holds out, vowing to fight three champions of Alba Longa to settle a war. At right the women of the family sink in grief, bound to the enemy by marriage and betrothal. David invented the oath scene himself, and its hard-edged clarity made it a model of Neoclassical painting.
artworks.lookCloser: Three arches frame three groups: sons, father, women. The father's hand gripping the swords sits just in front of the painting's vanishing point.

artworks.title: Bust of Nefertiti
artworks.medium: Painted limestone and stucco, quartz inlay
artworks.blurb: Nefertiti, chief wife of the pharaoh Akhenaten, wears her tall blue cap crown with a gold diadem band and a broad floral collar. The bust was found in 1912 in the Amarna workshop of the sculptor Thutmose and may have served as a model for other portraits. Egypt has sought its return since 1924, arguing that it left the country improperly.
artworks.lookCloser: Only the right eye has its quartz inlay; the left socket is bare limestone. CT scans revealed a subtly wrinkled face carved in the stone core beneath the smooth stucco.

artworks.title: The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa
artworks.blurb: Bernini shows the Spanish mystic Teresa of Ávila swooning on a cloud as an angel prepares to pierce her heart with a golden spear, following her own account of a vision. Made for Cardinal Federico Cornaro's burial chapel, the group is lit from a hidden window above. Its blend of spiritual and bodily rapture has been admired and attacked ever since.
artworks.lookCloser: On the side walls, marble members of the Cornaro family lean from boxes like theatregoers, discussing the vision. Gilded stucco rays stream down behind the figures.

artworks.title: View of Delft
artworks.blurb: Vermeer looked across the Kolk harbour at his home town from the south-east, with the Schiedam and Rotterdam gates reflected in still water beneath a vast, clouded sky. Sunlight picks out the tower of the Nieuwe Kerk, which he moved closer to the centre. It is his only cityscape, probably commissioned by his patron Pieter van Ruijven.
artworks.lookCloser: The initials VM appear on the barge at lower left. In Proust's novel, the writer Bergotte dies in front of this picture, admiring its "little patch of yellow wall".

artworks.title: The Death of Marat
artworks.collection: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, Brussels
artworks.blurb: The revolutionary journalist Jean-Paul Marat lies dead in the medicinal bath where he worked, stabbed by Charlotte Corday on 13 July 1793. David, his friend and fellow Montagnard, painted him within months as a secular martyr, the hanging arm recalling Christ in a Pietà, against a bare dark wall. His pupils made copies for the revolutionary cult of Marat.
artworks.lookCloser: Marat still holds a letter from Corday, its wording invented by David. The wooden block beside the tub is inscribed "À MARAT, DAVID".

artworks.title: Café Terrace at Night
artworks.blurb: Van Gogh set up his easel on the Place du Forum in Arles in September 1888 and painted this café terrace on the spot, at night. A large lantern floods the awning, facade and cobbles with yellow, set against a deep blue sky full of stars. It was his first starry sky, a year before The Starry Night.
artworks.lookCloser: There is no black anywhere: he called it "a painting of night without black". The stars are placed accurately enough for one scholar to date the scene to about 11 p.m.

artworks.title: Ginevra de' Benci
artworks.blurb: Leonardo painted the young Florentine Ginevra de' Benci, probably around her betrothal, pale and unsmiling against a dark juniper bush. The juniper, ginepro in Italian, puns on her name and stood for female virtue. The panel was cut down at the bottom, probably losing her hands, and it is the only painting by Leonardo on public view in the Americas.
artworks.lookCloser: The back of the panel is painted too: a juniper sprig inside a wreath of laurel and palm, with the motto VIRTVTEM FORMA DECORAT, "beauty adorns virtue".

artworks.title: Ghent Altarpiece
artworks.blurb: Commissioned by Joos Vijd and his wife Lysbette Borluut, this folding altarpiece was probably designed by Hubert van Eyck and painted largely by his younger brother Jan, who finished it in 1432. Opened on feast days, it shows God enthroned between Mary and John the Baptist, above a meadow where saints, prophets and pilgrims converge on the Lamb of God.
artworks.lookCloser: Light glints on the armour of the Knights of Christ and ripples across the Fountain of Life. At the far edges of the upper tier stand a naked Adam and Eve.

artworks.title: The Virgin and Child with Saint Anne
artworks.blurb: Mary sits on the lap of her mother, Saint Anne, and reaches for the infant Christ, who grips a lamb, a sign of his coming sacrifice. Leonardo worked on the panel for years and never finished it, locking the three figures into one group before a hazy mountain landscape. A cleaning in 2011 split experts over whether it left the picture too bright.
artworks.lookCloser: Freud claimed to see a vulture hidden in the Virgin's drapery, a theory built on a mistranslation: the bird in Leonardo's childhood memory was a kite.

artworks.title: Discobolus
artworks.medium: Marble, Roman copy of a lost bronze
artworks.collection: Museo Nazionale Romano, Palazzo Massimo, Rome
artworks.blurb: Myron's bronze discus thrower, made around 460–450 BCE, is lost, but Roman marble copies preserve it. This one, the Palombara or Lancellotti copy, was found on Rome's Esquiline Hill in 1781. The nude athlete is caught at the top of his backswing, body wound tight, yet his face stays calm and his torso shows no strain.
artworks.lookCloser: Hitler bought this copy in 1938 and showed it in Munich; it returned to Rome in 1948. Athletes still debate whether the pose would make an efficient throw.

artworks.title: Sistine Madonna
artworks.blurb: Pope Julius II commissioned this altarpiece for the monastery church of San Sisto in Piacenza. Parted green curtains reveal the Virgin standing on clouds with the Christ Child, between Pope Sixtus II and Saint Barbara, against a sky of faint angel faces. Bought for Dresden in 1754, it became a cult image for German writers from Goethe to Nietzsche.
artworks.lookCloser: At the bottom edge, two winged putti lean on their elbows and gaze upward. Lifted out of the picture, they have been reproduced on stamps, postcards and wrapping paper.

artworks.title: Netherlandish Proverbs
artworks.blurb: A crowded Flemish village acts out about 126 proverbs and idioms literally: people bang their heads against a wall, fill in a pond after the calf has died, and carry daylight in a basket. The picture's early title, The Blue Cloak or The Folly of the World, names Bruegel's real subject: human stupidity. His son Pieter the Younger painted at least 16 copies.
artworks.lookCloser: At the centre, a wife drapes a blue cloak over her husband, a sign that she is cuckolding him. Nearby, one man shears a sheep and another a pig.

artworks.title: The Blue Boy
artworks.collection: The Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens, San Marino
artworks.blurb: A youth in shimmering blue satin stands full-length against a stormy landscape. His costume was more than a century out of date: Gainsborough dressed him as a figure from Van Dyck's portraits. Long said to be Jonathan Buttall, a merchant's son, the sitter may instead be the painter's nephew Gainsborough Dupont. Before it left for California in 1922, 90,000 people saw it at the National Gallery in London.
artworks.lookCloser: At lower right, Gainsborough painted out a dog that once sat at the boy's feet. An X-ray revealed it in 1994, and infrared imaging shows the foliage he used to hide it.

artworks.title: The Night Café
artworks.collection: Yale University Art Gallery, New Haven
artworks.blurb: Van Gogh painted this all-night café in Arles over three nights in September 1888, sleeping during the day. Gaslight blazes from four lamps above a green billiard table, while a few customers slump at tables along blood-red walls. He wrote that he had tried to express "the terrible passions of humanity by means of red and green."
artworks.lookCloser: The landlord, Joseph Ginoux, stands beside the billiard table facing us. The painting's French title, Le Café de nuit, is written beneath the signature at lower right.

artworks.title: The Surrender of Breda
artworks.blurb: In 1625 the Dutch governor Justinus van Nassau hands the key of Breda to the Spanish commander Ambrogio Spinola, who lays a consoling hand on his shoulder. Velázquez painted it about ten years later for the Hall of Realms in Philip IV's Buen Retiro palace in Madrid. Victory is shown as courtesy rather than slaughter, with smoke from the siege drifting across the plain behind.
artworks.lookCloser: The tall, upright lances of the Spanish troops at right, which gave the picture its Spanish nickname Las lanzas, contrast with the few straggling Dutch pikes at left.

artworks.title: Benois Madonna
artworks.medium: Oil on canvas, transferred from panel
artworks.blurb: A young, laughing Virgin holds out a small sprig of flowers, and the Child on her lap reaches for it with intent concentration. It is probably one of two Madonnas Leonardo noted beginning in 1478, and possibly his first independent painting after Verrocchio's workshop. Long lost, it resurfaced with the Benois family in Saint Petersburg and was bought by the Hermitage in 1914.
artworks.lookCloser: The sprig the Child studies is shaped like a cross, a quiet foreshadowing of the Crucifixion. Behind them, a double-arched window opens onto nothing but pale blue sky.

artworks.title: The Coronation of Napoleon
artworks.blurb: In Notre-Dame on 2 December 1804, Napoleon, already wearing a golden laurel wreath, raises a crown over the kneeling Josephine while Pope Pius VII sits behind him, hand lifted in blessing. David, the emperor's official painter, worked on this canvas, almost ten metres wide, from 1805 to 1807. It is as much careful political stage-management as a record of the day.
artworks.lookCloser: Napoleon's mother sits in the central box, although she stayed away from the ceremony. Faint outlines show that David first painted Napoleon crowning himself.

artworks.title: Venus of Dolní Věstonice
artworks.blurb: A small nude woman with heavy breasts, belly and hips and only a slit-eyed hint of a face, modelled from local loess and fired at a low temperature about 30,000 years ago. Found in two pieces in 1925 at a mammoth hunters' settlement in Moravia, it is among the oldest known ceramic objects in the world.
artworks.lookCloser: A 2004 scan found a child's fingerprint fired into the surface. Four small holes in the top of the head may once have held feathers.

artworks.title: Benin Bronzes
artworks.collection: British Museum, London, and other collections
artworks.blurb: Thousands of cast brass plaques, heads and figures were made by a royal guild of casters for the Obas of Benin, in present-day Nigeria. The rectangular plaques, mostly cast in the 16th and 17th centuries, were nailed to the palace pillars and show the king, chiefs, warriors and Portuguese traders. British troops looted them in 1897, and several museums have since returned pieces to Nigeria.
artworks.lookCloser: On the plaques, rank sets size: the Oba or chief at the centre is larger than his attendants. Look too for Portuguese visitors, with their long hair, hats and European dress.

artworks.title: Mask of Agamemnon
artworks.blurb: A funeral mask hammered from a single sheet of gold, with a handlebar moustache and pointed beard. Heinrich Schliemann found it in 1876 in Shaft Grave V at Mycenae and believed he had gazed on the face of Homer's Agamemnon. It in fact dates to the 16th century BCE, centuries before any Trojan War, and a few scholars have questioned whether it is genuine.
artworks.lookCloser: The ears are cut out rather than engraved, and no other Mycenaean face has this beard and moustache: the very details at the heart of the authenticity debate.

artworks.title: Sleeping Venus
artworks.blurb: Venus sleeps naked in open country, one arm behind her head, the line of her body echoing the hills behind. Traditionally given to Giorgione, it was finished after his death in 1510 by Titian, who painted the landscape and, many now think, the figure too. It is the first known reclining nude in Western painting, and led directly to Titian's Venus of Urbino.
artworks.lookCloser: X-rays show a seated Cupid once sat at Venus's feet. It was painted over in the 19th century.

artworks.title: Saturn Devouring His Son
artworks.medium: Mural in mixed technique, transferred to canvas
artworks.blurb: A wild-eyed giant looms out of the dark, gripping a headless, bloodied body and about to take another bite. Goya painted it straight onto the dining-room wall of his house outside Madrid, the Quinta del Sordo, as one of fourteen Black Paintings never meant for public view. He left no title or notes; the murals were moved to canvas after his death.
artworks.lookCloser: The victim has an adult's proportions, not an infant's, and Saturn's usual attributes, such as a scythe or hourglass, are missing, so the traditional title has been questioned.

artworks.title: The Church at Auvers
artworks.blurb: Painted in June 1890, weeks before Van Gogh's death, this is the village church of Auvers-sur-Oise, north-west of Paris. He described it as violet against "a sky of simple deep blue colour, pure cobalt", its windows like ultramarine blotches. The sunlit sand in front contrasts with the church itself, which sits in its own shadow.
artworks.lookCloser: The path forks around the church, a motif Van Gogh used again in Wheat Field with Crows. A lone woman walks up the left-hand path.

artworks.title: The Red Vineyard
artworks.collection: Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow
artworks.blurb: Harvesters work among vines near Arles that have turned red in autumn, under a low, yellow evening sun. Van Gogh painted it in November 1888, while Gauguin was staying with him. In 1890 the Belgian painter Anna Boch bought it for 400 francs at the Les XX exhibition in Brussels, the only painting known by name that he sold in his lifetime.
artworks.lookCloser: Beyond the harvesters, the low sun is mirrored in a stretch of water, and a small horse-drawn carriage travels along the road.

artworks.title: The Yellow House
artworks.blurb: Van Gogh's rented house on Place Lamartine in Arles, painted in September 1888 under what he called "a sulphur sun" and "a pure cobalt sky". He hoped to make it a studio shared with other artists, and Gauguin lived there for nine weeks that autumn. The building was badly damaged in a bombing raid in 1944 and later demolished.
artworks.lookCloser: The first-floor corner window with both shutters open was the guest room Gauguin used. At the far right, a train crosses one of the railway bridges.

artworks.title: Apollo Belvedere
artworks.blurb: The god Apollo strides forward, having just loosed an arrow, perhaps at the serpent Python. This marble is a Roman copy of the 2nd century CE, probably after a lost bronze of about 330–320 BCE attributed to the Greek sculptor Leochares. Displayed in the Vatican's Belvedere courtyard from 1511, it was hailed by 18th-century Neoclassicists as the finest ancient sculpture.
artworks.lookCloser: The tree stump beside his right leg, with a snake coiled around it, is a support the heavy marble copy needed and the bronze original did not.

artworks.title: Barge Haulers on the Volga
artworks.blurb: Eleven men harnessed in leather straps drag a barge along the sandy bank of the Volga under a hot, hazy sky. Repin sketched real haulers in 1870 and chose them as a cross-section of Russia, including a former soldier, a defrocked priest and a painter. The finished picture made his name and became the best-known image of the Peredvizhniki's social realism.
artworks.lookCloser: In the centre, a youth in a pink shirt strains against his strap. Far off on the river, a tiny steamboat hints that this labour is becoming obsolete.

artworks.title: The Ninth Wave
artworks.blurb: After a night storm, a handful of shipwrecked men cling to a broken mast as another huge wave rears over them. In sailors' lore the ninth wave is the largest in a series. Aivazovsky, the prolific marine painter from Feodosia in Crimea, floods the scene with warm gold and green light, so that the rising sun offers hope as well as danger.
artworks.lookCloser: The wreckage the survivors hold forms a cross, often read as a sign of salvation.

artworks.title: Trundholm Sun Chariot
artworks.blurb: A bronze horse on wheels pulls a large disc, gilded on one side and also mounted on wheels. It probably shows the sun being drawn across the sky, and may have been rolled along during religious rituals. Cast locally around 1400 BCE, it was found in a peat bog on Trundholm moor, on the Danish island of Zealand, in 1902.
artworks.lookCloser: Only one face of the disc carries gold. It may show the bright day sun travelling west, with the dark side turned to the earth on its night journey back.

artworks.title: Aztec Sun Stone
artworks.collection: National Museum of Anthropology, Mexico City
artworks.blurb: A basalt disc about 3.6 metres across, carved in the Mexica capital Tenochtitlan during the reign of Moctezuma II. A central face, often identified as the sun god Tonatiuh, is framed by the four earlier eras of creation and a ring of twenty day signs. Buried after the Spanish conquest, it was dug up in Mexico City's main square in 1790.
artworks.lookCloser: The central figure clutches a human heart in each clawed hand, and his tongue is a stone sacrificial knife. Moctezuma II's name glyph is carved nearby.

artworks.title: Riace Bronzes
artworks.medium: Bronze with copper, silver and calcite inlays
artworks.collection: National Archaeological Museum of Magna Graecia, Reggio Calabria
artworks.blurb: Two bearded warriors, nude and slightly over life-size, found in the sea off Riace in southern Italy in 1972. They are rare surviving originals of Greek bronze sculpture: Statue A is usually dated about 460 BCE and Statue B about 430 BCE, probably by different sculptors. Their shields, spears and helmets are lost, and whom they represent is unknown.
artworks.lookCloser: Statue A bares a row of silver teeth between copper lips. His eyes are inlaid with calcite and his nipples with copper.

artworks.title: Royal Game of Ur
artworks.medium: Shell, red limestone and lapis lazuli inlay on wood
artworks.blurb: A board for a two-player race game, one of the oldest known, excavated by Leonard Woolley in the Royal Cemetery at Ur in southern Iraq. Twenty shell squares are set among red limestone and lapis lazuli. The game was played across the Middle East for more than two thousand years, and its rules were partly reconstructed from a Babylonian tablet of the 2nd century BCE.
artworks.lookCloser: Five of the squares carry rosettes. In Irving Finkel's reconstruction of the rules, landing on one gives the player an extra throw.

artworks.title: Saint John the Baptist
artworks.blurb: Saint John the Baptist emerges from near-total darkness, smiling and pointing up towards heaven. Probably Leonardo's last painting, it takes his sfumato to an extreme, with shadow melting into flesh without a visible edge. The soft, almost androgynous figure, possibly modelled on his pupil Salaì, has struck viewers as both devout and disquietingly sensual.
artworks.lookCloser: A thin reed cross, the saint's attribute, is held in his left hand and almost lost in the shadow. An animal pelt is draped across his shoulder.

artworks.title: Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I
artworks.medium: Oil, silver and gold leaf on canvas
artworks.blurb: Adele Bloch-Bauer, wife of the Viennese banker and sugar industrialist Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer, sits almost dissolved in a field of gold and silver leaf, with only her face, shoulders and hands painted naturalistically. It is the high point of Klimt's golden phase. Seized by the Nazis, it was returned to her niece Maria Altmann in 2006 after a seven-year legal fight.
artworks.lookCloser: Her dress is scattered with eye motifs drawn from ancient Egyptian art, and the jewelled choker at her neck also appears in Klimt's Judith.

artworks.title: La Belle Ferronnière
artworks.blurb: A young woman in a red dress looks past us from behind a stone parapet, her face modelled in soft light against a dark ground. Most scholars accept it as Leonardo's work from his years at the Sforza court in Milan, though other Milanese painters have been proposed. The sitter is unknown: Lucrezia Crivelli and Beatrice d'Este are the leading candidates.
artworks.lookCloser: The thin jewelled band across her forehead, a ferronnière, gave the painting its name. On her cheek and jaw, Leonardo painted a warm reflection of light from her red dress.

artworks.title: The Tempest
artworks.blurb: A young man with a staff stands at left; across a stream, a nearly naked woman nurses a baby, while lightning splits the sky over a town behind them. Made for the Venetian noble Gabriele Vendramin, it is one of the first Western paintings in which landscape and weather carry the mood. Its subject has never been securely explained.
artworks.lookCloser: X-rays show that Giorgione first painted a second nude woman where the man now stands. A stork perches on a rooftop at right.

artworks.title: Lion Man of the Hohlenstein-Stadel
artworks.blurb: A standing figure with a human body and the head of a cave lion, carved from mammoth ivory with a flint knife between about 41,000 and 35,000 years ago. It is one of the oldest known figurative sculptures, and an early sign of people imagining beings that do not exist. Found in a Swabian cave in 1939, its hundreds of fragments were pieced together over decades.
artworks.lookCloser: Seven parallel grooves are cut across the left arm. Their purpose is unknown.

artworks.title: Lindisfarne Gospels
artworks.blurb: A Latin gospel book made around 715–720 at the island monastery of Lindisfarne in Northumbria, probably by Eadfrith, Bishop of Lindisfarne, in honour of Saint Cuthbert. Its carpet pages weave Celtic knotwork, Anglo-Saxon animal interlace and Mediterranean models into dense patterns. In the 10th century the priest Aldred added an Old English gloss, the oldest surviving translation of the Gospels into English.
artworks.lookCloser: Between the Latin lines runs Aldred's tiny Old English translation in a different hand. On the decorated opening pages, letters are outlined with thousands of minute red dots.

artworks.title: Mask of Tutankhamun
artworks.medium: Gold inlaid with semi-precious stones and glass
artworks.blurb: The gold mask that lay over the mummy of the young king Tutankhamun, who died around 1323 BCE. Two layers of gold weighing over ten kilograms are inlaid with lapis lazuli, carnelian, quartz, obsidian and coloured glass, showing him in a striped nemes headcloth. Howard Carter's team uncovered it in 1925. Some Egyptologists think it was first made for another ruler, Neferneferuaten.
artworks.lookCloser: On the brow rise a vulture and a cobra, emblems of Upper and Lower Egypt. A spell from the Book of the Dead is inscribed across the shoulders and back.

artworks.title: Grande Odalisque
artworks.blurb: A concubine reclines with her back to us and looks over her shoulder, surrounded by silks, a peacock-feather fan and a pipe. Caroline Murat, Napoleon's sister and Queen of Naples, commissioned it. Critics mocked its anatomy, but Ingres lengthened the back and limbs on purpose, choosing smooth, sinuous line and cool, even light over literal accuracy.
artworks.lookCloser: Her back was said to have "two or three vertebrae too many". A modern study found that her left arm is also shorter than her right.

artworks.title: Moses
artworks.blurb: Moses sits with the tablets of the Law under his right arm, fingers twisting through his long beard, head turned sharply to one side. Michelangelo carved him for the tomb of Pope Julius II, a project first planned in 1505 with over forty statues and finished, much reduced, in 1545. Moses became the centrepiece of the final tomb.
artworks.lookCloser: The horns on his head follow the Latin Vulgate, which describes Moses' face as "horned" on his return from Sinai, a reading of a Hebrew word also understood as "shining".

artworks.title: Dying Gaul
artworks.blurb: A wounded Celtic warrior, naked but for a twisted torc at his neck, sits slumped on his fallen shield as blood runs from a wound in his side. This Roman marble copies a lost Hellenistic original, probably a bronze made around 230–220 BCE for Attalus I of Pergamon after his victory over the Galatians. It gives a defeated enemy unusual dignity.
artworks.lookCloser: His sword and a curved war trumpet lie beneath him, and his hair is stiff and matted: details that marked him as a Gaul, not the gladiator he was long taken for.

artworks.title: The Astronomer
artworks.blurb: A scholar in a loose robe leans from his desk to touch a celestial globe, lit by a leaded window. The globe is by Jodocus Hondius and the open book is Adriaan Metius's handbook of astronomy. Vermeer painted a companion, The Geographer, apparently of the same man in the same room; the model may be the Delft scientist Antonie van Leeuwenhoek.
artworks.lookCloser: The picture on the back wall shows the Finding of Moses, a figure associated with learning. There is no telescope in the room.

artworks.title: Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan
artworks.blurb: Tsar Ivan IV clutches his dying son on a blood-stained carpet, pressing a hand to the head wound he has just dealt him in a fit of rage. Repin, shaken by the assassination of Alexander II and the executions that followed, used the painter Grigoriy Myasoyedov and the writer Vsevolod Garshin as models. The canvas has been attacked twice, in 1913 and 2018.
artworks.lookCloser: The heavy staff Ivan struck with lies on the floor beside them. A single tear runs down the tsarevich's cheek.

artworks.title: Madonna of Bruges
artworks.blurb: The Virgin sits with lowered eyes while the Christ Child, standing between her knees, seems about to step away from her. In 1504 the Bruges cloth merchants Giovanni and Alessandro Mouscron bought it, and it became the first sculpture by Michelangelo to leave Italy in his lifetime. German troops took it in 1944; it was recovered from a salt mine at Altaussee.
