artworks.lookCloser: Mary's hand only loosely holds her son, and she does not look at him, as if she already knows where his steps will lead.

artworks.title: The Jewish Bride
artworks.blurb: A man rests his hand on a young woman's breast and she touches it lightly with her own, both dressed in glowing red and gold. Who they are is uncertain: the 19th-century title is now rejected, and they may be a couple portrayed as the biblical Isaac and Rebecca, a reading supported by an earlier Rembrandt drawing. It dates from his last years.
artworks.lookCloser: The man's golden sleeve is built up in thick, sculpted ridges of paint, some of it laid on with a palette knife.

artworks.title: The Sleepers
artworks.blurb: Two naked women lie asleep in each other's arms on a rumpled bed, one red-haired, one dark. Courbet painted it for the Ottoman diplomat and collector Halil Şerif Pasha, and one of the models was Joanna Hiffernan. It was a private commission: when a dealer showed it in 1872, it became the subject of a police report.
artworks.lookCloser: A broken pearl necklace and a hairpin lie scattered on the sheets, hints of what came before sleep.

artworks.title: The Yellow Christ
artworks.blurb: Breton women in traditional dress kneel at the foot of a yellow crucifix set among autumn fields near Pont-Aven. Gauguin painted it in 1889, placing the Crucifixion in contemporary Brittany as if it were the women's vision. Flat areas of yellow, red and green are held in dark outlines, the cloisonnist style he developed alongside Émile Bernard.
artworks.lookCloser: Gauguin based the figure of Christ on a painted wooden crucifix in the chapel of Trémalo, near Pont-Aven.

artworks.title: Virgin of Vladimir
artworks.collection: State Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow (on loan to the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour)
artworks.blurb: The Virgin presses her cheek to the Child's as he clings to her neck, an early example of the tender Eleousa type. Painted in Constantinople and sent to Kiev around 1131, the icon moved to Vladimir and then Moscow, where tradition credits it with saving the city from Timur in 1395. It became one of the most revered images in Russia.
artworks.lookCloser: Only the two faces are original. Compare their delicate modelling with the robes, which were repainted after fire and damage from a metal cover.

artworks.title: Lamentation over the Dead Christ
artworks.blurb: The dead Christ lies on a marble slab, seen from his feet, his body steeply foreshortened beneath a sheet. The Virgin, Saint John and Mary Magdalene weep at the left edge. Mantegna painted it probably in the early 1480s, in a restrained palette of browns and greys that makes the wounds in the hands and feet all the more shocking.
artworks.lookCloser: Mantegna made the feet smaller than true perspective demands. At their correct size they would hide much of the body.

artworks.title: The Art of Painting
artworks.blurb: Behind a heavy tapestry curtain, a painter in a slashed black doublet works on a picture of a young woman posed as Clio, Muse of History, with laurel wreath, trumpet and book. It is Vermeer's most complex allegory of his own art, and he never sold it. Hitler acquired it in 1940; after the war it went to the Kunsthistorisches Museum.
artworks.lookCloser: A crease runs down the large map of the Seventeen Provinces on the back wall, often read as the division between the Dutch Republic and the Spanish south.

artworks.title: The Storm on the Sea of Galilee
artworks.blurb: A fishing boat heels over as a wave breaks across its bow and the sail tears. In the light at left the disciples fight the rigging; in the shadowed stern others wake Christ, who will calm the storm. Painted in 1633, it is Rembrandt's only known seascape. It was stolen from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in 1990 and has never been recovered.
artworks.lookCloser: One man near the centre looks straight out at us and is usually taken as Rembrandt's self-portrait. Another disciple leans over the side, seasick.

artworks.title: Alexander Mosaic
artworks.blurb: This floor mosaic from the House of the Faun in Pompeii shows Alexander the Great, bareheaded on his horse Bucephalus, charging the Persian king Darius III, who turns in his chariot to flee. Laid in over a million tiny tesserae in reds, yellows, black and white, it probably copies a lost Greek painting of about 300 BCE, sometimes attributed to Philoxenus of Eretria.
artworks.lookCloser: Below Darius, a fallen Persian soldier sees his own dying face reflected in a polished shield. Nearby, a horse is shown from behind in steep foreshortening.

artworks.title: La Fornarina
artworks.collection: Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Antica (Palazzo Barberini), Rome
artworks.blurb: A young woman sits half-naked before a dark myrtle bush, one hand raised to her breast, a striped turban wound in her hair. Tradition names her Margherita Luti, the baker's daughter said to be Raphael's lover, but scholars also read her as an ideal beauty or a courtesan. The panel was probably still in his studio when he died in 1520.
artworks.lookCloser: Her armband is inscribed with the painter's name, RAPHAEL VRBINAS. X-rays found a ring on her left hand that was later painted over.

artworks.title: The Wedding Feast at Cana
artworks.blurb: Veronese turns the wedding where Christ changed water into wine into a Venetian banquet of some 130 guests in rich silks, framed by columns and a Palladian tower. The Benedictines of San Giorgio Maggiore commissioned it for their refectory and asked for the finest colours, including ultramarine. Napoleon's troops took it in 1797, and it is the largest painting in the Louvre.
artworks.lookCloser: In the foreground a group of musicians plays viols. A 17th-century tradition identifies them as Venetian painters: Veronese in white, Titian in red on the bass viol.

artworks.title: The Rokeby Venus
artworks.blurb: Venus lies with her back to us on dark sheets while Cupid holds up a mirror. It is Velázquez's only surviving female nude, a rare subject in Spain, where the Inquisition policed such images. Named after Rokeby Park in Yorkshire, where it hung in the 19th century, it was slashed by the suffragette Mary Richardson in 1914 and then restored.
artworks.lookCloser: The face in the mirror is blurred and far too large to be a true reflection of her. Pink silk ribbons loop over the mirror's frame.

artworks.title: The Little Street
artworks.blurb: An old brick house in Delft fills the canvas. A woman sews in the open doorway, two children kneel on the pavement, and down a side passage a maid bends over a barrel. It is one of only three views of his town Vermeer is known to have painted. Archival research in 2015 placed it on the Vlamingstraat, where the house belonged to his aunt.
artworks.lookCloser: Vermeer signed it "I V MEER" below the window at lower left. The whitewashed walls and patched brickwork are built up in thick paint you can almost feel.

artworks.title: The Triumph of Death
artworks.blurb: An army of skeletons sweeps across a burnt, barren landscape, herding the living into a coffin-shaped trap, cutting throats and hanging victims while ships sink offshore. Peasants, soldiers, lovers, a king and a cardinal all fall alike. Bruegel drew on the medieval Dance of Death and on Bosch to paint a panorama in which no one escapes.
artworks.lookCloser: At lower left, a dying king reaches for his barrels of coins while a skeleton holds up an hourglass. At lower right, a jester hides under the dinner table.

artworks.title: Whistler's Mother
artworks.blurb: Whistler's own title, Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1, insists this is a study in tone rather than a portrait. His mother, Anna McNeill Whistler, sits in profile against a grey wall in their Chelsea home, in a black dress and white cap. Shown at the Royal Academy in 1872 after nearly being rejected, it was bought by the French state in 1891.
artworks.lookCloser: The framed print on the wall is Whistler's own etching Black Lion Wharf. The dark patterned curtain at left is the only break in the grey and black.

artworks.title: When Will You Marry?
artworks.blurb: Two Tahitian women sit in a landscape of flat greens, yellows and blues. The one in front wears a traditional wrap and a white tiare flower behind her ear, perhaps a sign she is seeking a husband. Behind her, a woman in a high-necked Western dress raises a hand in a gesture linked to Buddhist art. Gauguin painted it on his first stay in Tahiti.
artworks.lookCloser: The Tahitian title, NAFEA Faa ipoipo, is painted at lower right. Gauguin often inscribed his Tahitian pictures, though he never got far beyond the basics of the language.

artworks.title: Doni Tondo
artworks.blurb: The only finished panel painting of Michelangelo's maturity shows the Holy Family as a tight, twisting group: a muscular Mary turns to pass or receive the Christ Child over her shoulder, with Joseph behind her. Beyond a low wall lounge five nude youths, and the young John the Baptist looks on. It was made for the Florentine merchant Agnolo Doni, probably for his marriage to Maddalena Strozzi.
artworks.lookCloser: The original carved frame, still attached, has five heads projecting into space, with the Strozzi family's crescent moons among its ornament.

artworks.title: Chimera of Arezzo
artworks.blurb: The fire-breathing monster of Greek myth, a lion with a goat's head rising from its back and a serpent for a tail, crouches and snarls, already wounded. It once formed part of a group with the hero Bellerophon, and an inscription marks it as an offering to the Etruscan god Tinia. Workmen found it at Arezzo in 1553, and Cosimo I de' Medici quickly claimed it.
artworks.lookCloser: The serpent tail biting the goat's horn is a restoration of 1785. An Etruscan inscription is engraved on the right foreleg.

artworks.title: David
artworks.blurb: The boy hero stands naked except for a laurel-topped hat and boots, Goliath's sword in hand and one foot on the giant's severed head. Probably made for the Medici, though its date is disputed, it is thought to be the first freestanding male nude since antiquity. The slender, almost androgynous body suggests a victory won through God's help, not strength.
artworks.lookCloser: A long wing from Goliath's helmet runs up the inside of David's right leg. Goliath's beard curls around the hero's sandalled foot.

artworks.title: The Return of the Prodigal Son
artworks.blurb: The ragged son kneels with his shaved head pressed against his old father, who rests both hands on his back. To the right the elder brother stands upright, lit but apart, and other figures watch from the shadows. Among Rembrandt's last works, painted within a year or two of his death in 1669, it turns the parable of forgiveness into near silence.
artworks.lookCloser: Compare the father's hands: the left is broad and masculine, the right slender and softer. One of the son's shoes has slipped off, baring a worn sole.

artworks.title: Morning in a Pine Forest
artworks.blurb: Mist hangs among tall pines as a mother bear and three cubs play on a snapped, fallen trunk. Ivan Shishkin painted the forest, and his friend Konstantin Savitsky added the bears. Pavel Tretyakov, who bought the picture, had Savitsky's signature removed, so it is usually credited to Shishkin alone. A sweet wrapper later made it one of the best-known images in Russia.
artworks.lookCloser: Look past the bears into the fog: the distant trunks fade from dark to pale as morning light filters through the forest.

artworks.title: The Beheading of Saint John the Baptist
artworks.blurb: In a bare prison yard the executioner pins John to the ground and reaches for a knife to finish the killing, while a jailer points and a servant girl holds out a golden dish for the head. Painted in Malta for the Knights of St John, it is Caravaggio's largest altarpiece. Months later he was expelled from the order in front of this same canvas.
artworks.lookCloser: Caravaggio's only known signature is written in the blood flowing from John's neck. At right, two prisoners watch through a barred window.

artworks.title: Charles IV of Spain and His Family
artworks.blurb: Goya lines up thirteen members of the Spanish royal family, life-size and glittering with sashes, jewels and silk. Queen María Luisa stands at the centre holding her youngest son's hand, with the king to the right and the future Ferdinand VII in blue at left. The debt to Velázquez's Las Meninas is open, but here there is no story, only people posing.
artworks.lookCloser: Goya painted himself in the shadows at far left, behind a large canvas. The young woman turning her face away is often read as Ferdinand's future bride, not yet known.

artworks.title: Las Hilanderas (The Spinners)
artworks.blurb: In a dim workshop women spin and wind wool; in a bright alcove behind, elegant ladies stand before a tapestry. Long read as a view of a royal tapestry works, it is now understood as Ovid's tale of Arachne, the weaver who challenged the goddess Athena. Most scholars date it to the late 1650s, though some argue for the 1640s.
artworks.lookCloser: The tapestry at the back copies Titian's Rape of Europa, then in the Spanish royal collection. The spokes of the spinning wheel at left dissolve into a blur of motion.

artworks.title: The Baptism of Christ
artworks.blurb: John the Baptist pours water over Christ in the River Jordan as the dove of the Holy Spirit descends between God's hands. The panel came from Andrea del Verrocchio's Florentine workshop, and his young pupil Leonardo da Vinci painted the kneeling angel at far left and, many scholars think, much of the hazy landscape behind.
artworks.lookCloser: Compare the two angels: Leonardo's, turned away from us, has softer modelling and hair than its companion. John's scroll reads "ECCE AGNIUS".

artworks.title: The Death of Sardanapalus
artworks.blurb: Facing defeat, the Assyrian king Sardanapalus reclines on a vast red bed and watches, unmoved, as his servants kill his concubines and horses before the palace burns. Inspired by Byron's play, Delacroix painted the scene in hot reds and golds with loose, rushing brushwork. It was attacked at the Salon of 1827, one critic calling it "the fanaticism of ugliness".
artworks.lookCloser: Golden elephant heads decorate the foot of the bed. At lower left, a man drives a knife into a richly harnessed horse.

artworks.title: The Painter's Studio
artworks.blurb: Courbet sits at the centre of his studio painting a landscape of his native Ornans, watched by a nude model and a boy. To the left crowd figures from ordinary life; to the right stand his friends and supporters, among them Baudelaire, Proudhon and his patron Alfred Bruyas. He subtitled it "a real allegory" and, when the 1855 World Fair rejected it, showed it in his own Pavilion of Realism.
artworks.lookCloser: At the far right, Baudelaire sits absorbed in a book. A white cat plays at the painter's feet.

artworks.title: Luncheon of the Boating Party
artworks.blurb: Renoir's friends linger after lunch on the balcony of the Maison Fournaise, a restaurant on the Seine at Chatou, beneath a striped awning. Wine, fruit and glasses catch the light on the table while men in singlets and boaters talk and flirt. Renoir combined figures, still life and landscape in one canvas, and critics singled it out at the 1882 Impressionist exhibition.
artworks.lookCloser: At lower left, the seamstress Aline Charigot, later Renoir's wife, plays with a small affenpinscher. Gustave Caillebotte sits astride a chair at lower right.

artworks.title: The Blind Leading the Blind
artworks.blurb: Six blind men, linked by their staffs, stumble along a village path. The leader has already toppled into a ditch and the rest seem bound to follow. Bruegel painted Christ's parable from Matthew 15:14 the year before his death, in thin, glue-based paint on linen, and the falling diagonal turns a proverb into a slow collapse.
artworks.lookCloser: Each man's eyes show a different condition, painted precisely enough for doctors to identify them. The church behind is that of Sint-Anna-Pede, near Brussels.

artworks.title: L'Absinthe
artworks.blurb: A woman sits in a Paris café with a glass of pale green absinthe, staring at nothing, beside a man in a hat who looks away out of the frame. The models were friends, the actress Ellen Andrée and the painter and etcher Marcellin Desboutin, posed in the Nouvelle-Athènes. Shown in London in 1893, it was condemned as degraded and read as a warning about drink.
artworks.lookCloser: The café tables have no visible legs; their bare tops zigzag across the foreground and push the pair into the upper right. Their shadowy reflections appear in the mirror behind.

artworks.title: The Hay Wain
artworks.blurb: A hay wagon drawn by three horses fords the River Stour near Flatford Mill in Suffolk, beneath a sky of moving summer cloud, with Willy Lott's cottage at left. First shown in 1821 as Landscape: Noon, it failed to sell in London but won a gold medal at the Paris Salon of 1824, where it impressed Delacroix and a generation of French painters.
artworks.lookCloser: A dog on the near bank watches the wagon. Flecks of white paint catch the light on water and leaves, a device critics called "Constable's snow".

artworks.title: Venus of Brassempouy
artworks.blurb: This thumb-sized ivory head, found in 1894 in the Grotte du Pape at Brassempouy in southwest France, is one of the earliest realistic human faces known. Carved about 25,000 years ago, it has a long neck, a straight nose and a strong brow, but no mouth. It was probably broken from a larger figure, and whether it shows a woman is uncertain.
artworks.lookCloser: A grid of shallow cuts covers the head, read as a hood, a wig or braided hair. A vertical crack on the right follows the grain of the ivory.

artworks.title: Alexander Sarcophagus
artworks.medium: Pentelic marble with traces of paint
artworks.blurb: Not Alexander's tomb, but a marble coffin from the royal necropolis at Sidon, probably made for Abdalonymus, the king Alexander installed there in 332 BCE, though some argue for a Persian governor. Its reliefs show Alexander fighting Persians at the Battle of Issus on one side and Macedonians and Persians hunting lions together on the other. Much of its original paint survives.
artworks.lookCloser: On the battle side, Alexander charges on horseback wearing a lion's scalp as a helmet, the emblem of Heracles. Look for traces of original colour on the cloaks and saddlecloths.

artworks.title: Venus of Hohle Fels
artworks.blurb: Carved from mammoth tusk between 42,000 and 40,000 years ago, this palm-sized figure is the oldest undisputed image of a human being. Her breasts, belly and vulva are hugely enlarged, her short arms rest on her stomach, and she has no head. Archaeologists from Tübingen found her in 2008 in a cave in southwest Germany, close to a flute made from a vulture bone.
artworks.lookCloser: In place of a head is a pierced loop, so the figure may have been worn as a pendant. Fine incised lines run across the belly and arms.

artworks.title: Augustus of Prima Porta
artworks.blurb: Rome's first emperor raises his arm to address his troops, in the balanced stance of a Greek athlete and with the ageless face of his official portraits. Found in 1863 at the villa of his widow Livia at Prima Porta, the marble is probably a copy of a lost bronze. His bare feet hint at divine status.
artworks.lookCloser: At the centre of the breastplate a Parthian hands back a captured Roman standard, recalling Augustus's diplomatic triumph of 20 BCE. A small Cupid rides a dolphin beside his right leg.

artworks.title: Standard of Ur
artworks.medium: Shell, red limestone and lapis lazuli on wood (reconstructed)
artworks.blurb: Excavated by Leonard Woolley in the late 1920s from a royal tomb at Ur, in present-day Iraq, this box is inlaid on each side with shell figures set against lapis lazuli. One face shows war, with wagons trampling enemies and prisoners led before the king; the other shows peace, with animals and goods brought to a banquet. Woolley called it a standard, but its purpose is unknown.
artworks.lookCloser: On both sides the king is the tallest figure, his head breaking through the top border. At the banquet, a musician plays a lyre.

artworks.title: The Burial of the Count of Orgaz
artworks.blurb: Saints Stephen and Augustine, in gold vestments, lower the armoured body of a 14th-century nobleman into his tomb, while a row of black-clad Toledan gentlemen looks on. Above, an angel carries his soul up through the clouds towards Christ, the Virgin and John the Baptist. El Greco painted it for the church where the count is buried, and it still hangs there.
artworks.lookCloser: The boy at lower left is El Greco's son Jorge Manuel. The handkerchief in his pocket carries the painter's signature and the date 1578, the year of the boy's birth.

artworks.title: The Supper at Emmaus
artworks.blurb: The risen Christ, beardless and unrecognised, blesses bread at an inn table, and in that instant two disciples know him: one flings his arms wide, the other pushes back his chair to rise. The innkeeper, standing, notices nothing. Painted in Rome for Ciriaco Mattei, it sets the miracle among ordinary things, hard-lit against a dark wall.
artworks.lookCloser: The fruit basket is perched on the very edge of the table, as if about to fall into our space. Its shadow has been read as a fish, an early symbol of Christ.

artworks.title: The Peasant Wedding
artworks.blurb: A wedding feast crowds a barn at harvest time. Two men carry bowls of porridge on a door taken off its hinges, pipers play, and the bride sits before a green hanging under a paper crown, eyes half-closed. Which man is the groom is still argued over. Bruegel observed such customs closely enough that the scene is used as evidence of 16th-century peasant life.
artworks.lookCloser: In the foreground a small child licks a plate clean. The servant in red carrying the door appears to have three feet; the third belongs to a man behind him.

artworks.title: A Young Girl Reading
artworks.collection: National Gallery of Art, Washington, DC
artworks.blurb: A girl in a lemon-yellow dress sits in profile against a violet cushion, absorbed in a small book held in one hand. Her name is unknown: the picture belongs to Fragonard's fantasy figures, painted quickly and freely rather than as formal portraits. Warm yellows and fast, visible strokes make a private moment feel full of light.
artworks.lookCloser: Fragonard scratched the folds of her white ruff into the wet paint with the wooden end of his brush. X-rays show that a first head turned towards the viewer.

artworks.title: A Philosopher Lecturing on the Orrery
artworks.collection: Derby Museum and Art Gallery, Derby
artworks.blurb: A lecturer demonstrates an orrery, a clockwork model of the solar system, to a small group gathered in the dark. A lamp standing in for the Sun lights their faces, from rapt children to a man taking notes. Joseph Wright of Derby gave a scientific demonstration the solemn, candlelit awe once reserved for religious painting.
artworks.lookCloser: The lamp itself is hidden behind the silhouetted boy in the foreground. The man taking notes is thought to be Wright's friend, the mapmaker Peter Perez Burdett.

artworks.title: The Massacre at Chios
artworks.blurb: Greek civilians, wounded, exhausted or dying, wait in the foreground while an Ottoman horseman rears above them and a ruined landscape stretches behind. Delacroix responded to the 1822 massacre on Chios, where some twenty thousand people were killed and most survivors enslaved. Shown at the Salon of 1824, it offers no hero and no hope.
artworks.lookCloser: At lower right, a baby reaches for the breast of its dead mother. The old woman beside them stares past the scene.

artworks.title: Medusa
artworks.medium: Oil on canvas mounted on a convex wooden shield
artworks.blurb: The Gorgon's severed head screams from a round parade shield, snakes writhing from her scalp and blood spurting from her neck. Cardinal del Monte commissioned it as a gift for Ferdinando I de' Medici. Caravaggio painted on a curved surface yet made the head seem to project forward, and the face is often said to be his own.
artworks.lookCloser: The head casts a shadow on the pale green ground, as though it floated before a flat surface, though the shield actually bulges outward.

artworks.title: Madonna of the Goldfinch
artworks.blurb: Mary sits in a spring landscape with a book, while the infant John the Baptist offers a goldfinch to the Christ Child, who reaches to stroke it. The three figures form a calm pyramid learned from Leonardo. Raphael painted it in Florence as a wedding gift for his friend Lorenzo Nasi; in 1548 a landslide shattered it into seventeen pieces.
artworks.lookCloser: The goldfinch, which feeds among thistles, was a traditional sign of Christ's Passion. Mary holds a small open book in her left hand.

artworks.title: Judith Beheading Holofernes
artworks.collection: Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Antica (Palazzo Barberini), Rome
artworks.blurb: Judith draws a sword through the neck of the Assyrian general Holofernes, gripping his hair at arm's length, her brow creased between resolve and disgust. Her old maid Abra waits beside her. Caravaggio set the killing on a shallow stage lit from the side against black, and the picture shaped later versions by Artemisia Gentileschi. Its date is debated, between about 1599 and 1602.
artworks.lookCloser: Compare Judith's smooth young face, probably modelled by the courtesan Fillide Melandroni, with the wrinkled profile of Abra beside her.

artworks.title: The Three Philosophers
artworks.blurb: Three men of different ages, an old bearded sage, a turbaned man and a seated youth, pause at the edge of a wood before a dark cave, with a village and hills in soft light behind. One of Giorgione's last works, possibly painted for Taddeo Contarini, it has been read as the Magi, as stages of philosophy and as Plato's cave. No reading has won.
artworks.lookCloser: The young man holds a set square and compass as he studies the cave. The canvas has been cut down on the left, beside the rock face.

artworks.title: The Abbey in the Oakwood
artworks.blurb: Monks carry a coffin through snow towards a ruined Gothic church, modelled on Eldena Abbey, framed by bare oaks against a pale dusk sky. Friedrich showed it in Berlin in 1810 hung beneath his Monk by the Sea, and the Prussian king bought both. Death, ruin and the fading day meet in a single wintry image.
artworks.lookCloser: A freshly dug grave opens in the snow in the foreground among leaning crosses. Two tiny candles light the procession, and a crescent moon hangs in the sky.

artworks.title: Amor Vincit Omnia
artworks.blurb: A grinning, naked Cupid with dark eagle's wings clambers off a table, trampling the emblems of human achievement: musical instruments, armour, a crown, a compass and a manuscript. Painted for the collector Vincenzo Giustiniani, who reportedly prized it above all his pictures, it illustrates Virgil's line "Love conquers all". Its frank realism provoked a rival answer from Giovanni Baglione.
artworks.lookCloser: On the sheet of music on the floor, look for a large V, possibly a nod to Vincenzo Giustiniani. The wings were painted from props lent by Orazio Gentileschi.

artworks.title: The Clothed Maja
artworks.blurb: A young woman in a tight white dress, short jacket and pink sash reclines on green cushions and looks straight at us. Goya painted this clothed version after The Nude Maja, and the pair first surface in 1808 in the seized collection of the minister Manuel Godoy. Whether she is the Duchess of Alba or Godoy's mistress Pepita Tudó is still debated.
artworks.lookCloser: Compare her with her nude twin: the same pose, arms folded behind the head, but here the dress is painted with loose, quick strokes. The Inquisition seized both pictures in 1814.

artworks.title: View of Toledo
artworks.collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
artworks.blurb: El Greco sets Toledo high on a green ridge beneath a storm-dark sky, its pale buildings flaring against the clouds. Landscape was rare in Spanish painting, and this one bends the facts: several landmarks are moved to suit the composition. It reads less as a map than as a portrait of a city of the spirit, raised on its hill like a pedestal.
artworks.lookCloser: The Castle of San Servando on the left is placed accurately; several other landmarks are not. The artist signed in Greek letters, lower right, as Domenikos Theotokopoulos.

artworks.title: The Magpie on the Gallows
artworks.blurb: Peasants dance to bagpipes beside a gallows where a magpie perches, while a vast river valley opens behind them into blue distance. Painted the year after the Duke of Alba arrived to crush dissent in the Netherlands, it plays on proverbs about gossip and about dancing on the gallows. It is among the last pictures Bruegel painted before his death in 1569.
artworks.lookCloser: The gallows is an impossible object: its posts stand side by side, yet the crossbeam recedes into space. In the shadows at far left, a man relieves himself.

artworks.title: The Marriage of the Virgin
artworks.blurb: Joseph slips a ring onto Mary's finger before the high priest, flanked by her companions and the rejected suitors. The 21-year-old Raphael based this altarpiece for San Francesco in Città di Castello on a composition by his teacher Perugino, then surpassed it: the domed, many-sided temple behind sets the whole piazza into clear, measured space.
artworks.lookCloser: A disappointed suitor snaps his barren rod across his knee in the foreground. Raphael signed and dated the temple frieze: RAPHAEL VRBINAS MDIIII.

artworks.title: Young Sick Bacchus
artworks.blurb: The wine god wears a vine wreath and a bare shoulder, but his lips are grey and his skin sallow. According to Caravaggio's first biographer, the young painter made it with a mirror, so this is himself, early in his Roman years, when he reportedly spent months in hospital. It also advertised his skill at still life, portraiture and the antique.
artworks.lookCloser: The grapes and peaches on the stone ledge are studied as closely as the face. Cardinal Scipione Borghese seized the picture from the painter Cavalier d'Arpino in 1607.

artworks.title: Apollo and Daphne
artworks.blurb: Apollo catches the nymph Daphne at the instant she turns into a laurel tree, as Ovid tells it. Bark is already closing over her legs, leaves burst from her fingers and her mouth opens in alarm. Bernini carved it in his early twenties for Cardinal Scipione Borghese, with his assistant Giuliano Finelli cutting some of the finest leaves and twigs.
artworks.lookCloser: Her toes are turning into roots that grip the rock. On the base, a moralising couplet by Maffeo Barberini, the future Pope Urban VIII, justifies the pagan chase.

artworks.title: Doryphoros (Spear-Bearer)
artworks.medium: Marble, Roman copy after a lost bronze original
artworks.blurb: A muscular young man steps forward, weight on his right leg, his left hand once gripping a spear on his shoulder. Polykleitos made the bronze original around 440 BCE to demonstrate his treatise on ideal proportion, the Canon. It survives only in Roman marbles like this one from Pompeii, and its relaxed contrapposto shaped Western sculpture for centuries.
artworks.lookCloser: The tree stump behind the leg and the strut at the right wrist are the copyist's additions: marble needs props that the bronze original did without.

artworks.title: The Sea of Ice
artworks.blurb: Slabs of pack ice pile up into a jagged tower under a pale sky, and only slowly do we notice the hull of a crushed ship. Friedrich never saw the Arctic; he made oil studies of ice floes on the Elbe and probably knew of Parry's polar expeditions. Radical in its bareness, the picture baffled viewers and was still unsold at his death.
artworks.lookCloser: Find the wrecked ship, half-swallowed by the ice on the right. The foreground slabs rise like a staircase toward the summit.

artworks.title: The Balcony
artworks.blurb: Three of Manet's friends pose behind green railings: the painter Berthe Morisot, seated, the painter Antoine Guillemet and the violinist Fanny Claus. None looks at another, and a boy, probably Léon Leenhoff, glimmers in the dark room behind. Loosely based on Goya's Majas on a Balcony, it puzzled critics at the Salon of 1869.
artworks.lookCloser: Below Morisot's chair a small dog plays with a ball. Guillemet's blue tie and her red fan are the only strong accents in a palette of white, green and black.

artworks.title: The Descent from the Cross
artworks.blurb: Ten near life-size figures crowd a shallow gilded niche as Christ's body is lowered from the cross, and the Virgin swoons in a pose that echoes her son's. Rogier van der Weyden painted it for the crossbowmen's guild of Leuven, making it look like a painted, carved altarpiece. It became the most copied Netherlandish image of the subject.
artworks.lookCloser: Tiny crossbows, the guild's emblem, hang in the gilded tracery of the upper corners. Then look for the glassy tears on the mourners' faces.

artworks.title: Death of the Virgin
artworks.blurb: The Virgin lies dead in a plain red dress, her head lolling and feet bare and swollen, while the apostles bow their heads and Mary Magdalene weeps on a low chair. Commissioned for a Carmelite church in Rome, it was rejected as indecorous, and rumour said a courtesan had posed. Rubens then advised the Duke of Mantua to buy it.
artworks.lookCloser: Her halo is only a thin gold line. A huge blood-red curtain billows overhead, picking up the colour of her dress.

artworks.title: Girl Reading a Letter at an Open Window
artworks.blurb: A young woman reads a letter by an open window, her face reflected faintly in the glass, with a bowl of fruit tipped on the rug before her. For centuries the wall behind her was blank. A restoration completed in 2021 removed later overpaint to reveal Vermeer's own picture of Cupid, which makes it almost certainly a love letter.
artworks.lookCloser: The green curtain at right seems to hang in front of the painting itself. Tiny dots of light glint on the fruit and in her hair.

artworks.title: Woman Holding a Balance
artworks.collection: National Gallery of Art, Washington, DC
artworks.blurb: A woman in a fur-trimmed blue jacket holds a small balance over a table strewn with pearls and gold, lit by a curtained window. Behind her hangs a painting of the Last Judgment. Once called Woman Weighing Gold, it is now read as a call to temperance, though whether she is pregnant or simply fashionably dressed is still argued.
artworks.lookCloser: Both pans of the balance are empty, and they hang perfectly level.

artworks.title: Portrait of an Unknown Woman
artworks.blurb: A young woman in dark velvet, fur and leather gloves looks down at us from an open carriage on a winter street in St Petersburg. Kramskoi, a leader of the Peredvizhniki, never named her, and early critics took her for a courtesan. The mystery made her famous, and she has often stood in for Anna Karenina on book covers.
artworks.lookCloser: The setting is the Anichkov Bridge, but the city behind her dissolves into pale, frosty haze, so her dark figure fills the picture.

artworks.title: The Sleeping Gypsy
artworks.collection: The Museum of Modern Art, New York
artworks.blurb: Under a full moon in an empty desert, a woman in a striped robe sleeps beside her mandolin and water jar while a lion sniffs at her but does not attack. Henri Rousseau, a self-taught painter who had worked in the Paris toll service, called the moonlight effect 'very poetic'. He tried and failed to sell it to his home town of Laval.
artworks.lookCloser: Her rainbow-striped robe and blanket are flat bands of colour, and the smooth sand shows no footprints, as if sleeper and lion simply appeared there.

artworks.title: Assumption of the Virgin
artworks.collection: Basilica di Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari, Venice
artworks.blurb: The apostles surge and gesture below as the Virgin rises on a cloud of angels toward God the Father, through three zones of ever brighter golden light. Unveiled on the Frari's high altar in May 1518, Titian's first great public commission brought Roman grandeur to Venice. At nearly seven metres tall, it is the city's largest altarpiece.
artworks.lookCloser: Titian signed TITIANUS on the sarcophagus beneath Saint Peter. From the back of the nave, the arched top sits exactly inside the arch of the stone choir screen.

artworks.title: The Turkish Bath
artworks.medium: Oil on canvas mounted on panel
artworks.blurb: A crowd of nude women lounge, bathe and play music in an imagined harem, seen as if through a round window. Ingres, who never travelled to the East, reassembled bathers and odalisques from half a century of his own work, then turned the rectangular picture into a tondo. He finished it at 82 and proudly inscribed his age.
artworks.lookCloser: The lute player with her back to us is his Valpinçon Bather of 1808, reused almost unchanged. Find the inscription AETATIS LXXXII, 'aged 82'.

artworks.title: Venus and Mars
artworks.blurb: Venus, fully dressed and wide awake, watches Mars sprawl in exhausted sleep while infant satyrs play with his lance and helmet. The long format suggests it was set into panelling or furniture in a bedroom, probably to celebrate a marriage. Its learned joke, love disarming war, draws on Lucian's description of a lost ancient painting.
artworks.lookCloser: Wasps buzz around Mars's head from a nest in the tree, perhaps a pun on the Vespucci family, whose name means 'little wasps'. A satyr blows a conch in his ear.

artworks.title: Danaë
artworks.blurb: A life-size nude raises her hand toward a flood of golden light as an old servant draws back the bed curtain. In Greek myth Zeus came to the imprisoned Danaë as a shower of gold; Rembrandt shows only the light. He reworked her head, arm and legs years later. In 1985 an attacker threw acid on the canvas, and restoration took twelve years.
artworks.lookCloser: Above the bed, a gilded carved Cupid weeps, his hands bound.

artworks.title: The Barque of Dante
artworks.blurb: Dante, in a red hood, recoils as the damned claw at the boat carrying him and Virgil across the Styx toward the burning city of Dis, a scene from Canto VIII of the Inferno. It was the young Delacroix's first Salon picture. Gros praised it as 'a chastened Rubens', and the state bought it for 2,000 francs.
artworks.lookCloser: Water drops on the bodies of the damned are separate touches of pure red, yellow, green and white, an early sign of Delacroix's thinking about colour.

artworks.title: The Last Day of Pompeii
artworks.blurb: Lightning flashes and statues topple over a Pompeii street as families flee Vesuvius in AD 79, each group a small drama of rescue or loss. Bryullov set it on the Street of the Tombs, which he had studied on site, and joined classical figures to Romantic colour. Acclaimed in Rome, Milan and Paris, it made him the first Russian painter with a European reputation.
artworks.lookCloser: At the left of the fleeing crowd, Bryullov painted himself carrying a box of painting materials on his head.

artworks.title: Along the River During the Qingming Festival
artworks.medium: Ink and colour on silk, handscroll
artworks.blurb: Unrolled from right to left, this five-metre handscroll moves from quiet farmland into the crowded commerce of the Northern Song capital, Bianjing, today's Kaifeng. More than 800 people fill its boats, bridges, shops and inns. Attributed to Zhang Zeduan, though its date and purpose are still debated, it was copied hundreds of times by later painters.
artworks.lookCloser: At the Rainbow Bridge, a cargo boat swings toward the span with its mast not yet lowered. Crowds shout, and someone on the bridge lowers a rope to the crew.

artworks.title: Sacred and Profane Love
artworks.blurb: Two women who look like sisters sit on a carved marble fountain: one richly dressed as a bride, the other nude but for a red cloak, holding up a smoking vessel. A winged boy stirs the water between them. Probably painted for Niccolò Aurelio's wedding, it has carried its title only since 1693, and its meaning is still debated.
artworks.lookCloser: Aurelio's coat of arms is carved on the front of the fountain. Two rabbits, emblems of fertility, sit in the landscape behind the clothed woman.

artworks.title: An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump
artworks.blurb: By the light of a single hidden candle, a travelling lecturer pumps the air from a glass flask holding a white cockatoo while his audience reacts: two girls cannot bear to watch, a young couple see only each other, a man times the experiment. Wright gave a scientific demonstration the gravity of a religious scene, and left the bird's fate open.
artworks.lookCloser: A full moon shows through the window, where a boy handles the empty cage. Behind the candle, a human skull sits in a glass vessel of liquid.

artworks.title: Belshazzar's Feast
artworks.blurb: A hand emerges from a cloud to write on the wall, and the Babylonian king Belshazzar turns in terror, his jewelled turban glinting, as wine spills from vessels looted from the Temple in Jerusalem. It is the young Rembrandt's bid to make his name with large, theatrical history painting, and its palette is unusually rich for him.
artworks.lookCloser: The Hebrew letters run in vertical columns rather than right-to-left rows, perhaps why Babylon's wise men could not read them. Rembrandt took them from his friend Menasseh ben Israel.

artworks.title: The Madonna of Chancellor Rolin
artworks.blurb: Nicolas Rolin, chancellor of Burgundy, kneels at a prayer desk facing the Virgin and Child as an angel lowers a crown onto her head. Beyond the columned loggia, a river city stretches toward blue mountains in minute detail. Painted for Rolin's parish church in Autun, it shows the chancellor, unusually, at the same scale as the Virgin.
artworks.lookCloser: On the battlements beyond the garden, two tiny men look out over the river. The one in the red hat may be van Eyck himself.

artworks.title: Bacchus
artworks.blurb: A plump youth crowned with vine leaves reclines on a couch, fingering the black bow of his robe and offering a brimming goblet of wine. Painted for Cardinal Francesco Maria del Monte, it is both the god Bacchus and a Roman boy in costume. The fruit bowl, with a split pomegranate and a spoiled apple, hints that pleasure fades.
artworks.lookCloser: In 2009, reflectography confirmed a tiny figure of a painter at his easel reflected on the glass carafe, thought to be Caravaggio himself. It is invisible to the naked eye.

artworks.title: Rain, Steam and Speed – The Great Western Railway
artworks.blurb: A steam train charges toward us across Brunel's Maidenhead Railway Bridge over the Thames, its dark engine almost dissolved in rain, mist and golden light. Turner, then nearly seventy, made modern speed itself the subject, building the picture from thin veils of colour and thick palette-knife work. It was first shown at the Royal Academy in 1844.
artworks.lookCloser: A hare races ahead of the train along the track, lower right. On the river at left, a small boat drifts past.

artworks.title: The Rape of Proserpina
artworks.blurb: Pluto, god of the underworld, hoists the struggling Proserpina as three-headed Cerberus guards the threshold at his feet. Bernini finished the group at 23 for Cardinal Scipione Borghese, who soon gave it to Ludovico Ludovisi, nephew of the new pope. Designed to be read in full from the front, it makes hard marble behave like yielding flesh.
artworks.lookCloser: Pluto's fingers sink into her thigh as if into soft skin, and tears run down her cheek as she pushes his face away.

artworks.title: Portrait of the Four Tetrarchs
artworks.blurb: Four armoured emperors embrace in pairs, each with a hand on his sword hilt, their faces almost identical. They stand for the Tetrarchy, Diocletian's shared rule by two senior and two junior emperors, rather than for individuals. Carved in purple porphyry from Egypt, a stone reserved for emperors, they were looted from Constantinople in 1204 and set into a corner of St Mark's.
artworks.lookCloser: One emperor is missing part of his foot. The heel was found in Istanbul in the 1960s and is now in the city's Archaeology Museum.

artworks.title: Charioteer of Delphi
artworks.blurb: A young driver stands calm in a long pleated tunic, reins still in his hand, after a chariot victory at the Pythian Games. He once rode in a bronze chariot with horses, dedicated to Apollo by Polyzalos, tyrant of Gela in Sicily. Buried under rockfall, probably in the earthquake of 373 BCE, he is one of the few Greek bronzes to survive.
artworks.lookCloser: He keeps his inlaid glass eyes, a rare survival. The deep pleats of his lower tunic fall straight, like the fluting of a column.

artworks.title: The Geographer
artworks.blurb: A young scholar in a Japanese-style robe leans over a chart, dividers in hand, and gazes toward the window as if struck by an idea. The globe, sea chart and cross-staff are accurate tools of his trade. It pairs with Vermeer's Astronomer, painted with the same model; the Delft scientist Antonie van Leeuwenhoek has been proposed but never proven.
artworks.lookCloser: The globe is a 1618 Hondius, turned to the Indian Ocean, where the Dutch East India Company traded. This is one of only three paintings Vermeer both signed and dated.

artworks.title: Woman in Blue Reading a Letter
artworks.blurb: A woman in a blue jacket stands absorbed in a letter, lit from an unseen window, before a large map of Holland. No corner, floor or ceiling is visible, only wall, chairs and table, so all attention falls on her stillness. Whether her full figure signals pregnancy or fashion is debated, and the letter's writer is left to us.
artworks.lookCloser: The map is a real one, Van Berckenrode's Holland and West Friesland, reissued by Blaeu in 1621. On the table, pearls lie by an open box.

artworks.title: Music in the Tuileries
artworks.collection: National Gallery, London, and Hugh Lane Gallery, Dublin
artworks.blurb: Fashionable Parisians gather under the trees of the Tuileries for an afternoon concert, though no musicians appear. Manet filled the crowd with friends, among them Baudelaire, Gautier, Fantin-Latour, Offenbach and his brother Eugène. Its quick, sketchy handling and modern subject angered visitors in 1863, and it pointed the way for Monet and Renoir.
artworks.lookCloser: Manet included himself at the far left edge, beside the painter Albert de Balleroy. The iron chairs in the foreground had only just replaced wooden ones in the gardens.

artworks.title: The Ship of Fools
artworks.blurb: A crowded little boat drifts nowhere, crewed by a friar, a nun and peasants who sing, drink and grab at food, with a leafy tree for a mast. The panel is a fragment of a triptych wing; its lower part, an Allegory of Gluttony, is at Yale. It mocks gluttony and folly, echoing Sebastian Brant's popular satire Das Narrenschiff.
artworks.lookCloser: The friar and nun gape at a pancake dangling on a string between them. Up in the leafy mast an owl peers out, and a jester sits apart, drinking.

artworks.title: Adoration of the Magi
artworks.blurb: The Holy Family sits on a ruined classical building as the three kings kneel with gifts, surrounded by Florentines in fine clothes. Commissioned by the banker Gaspare del Lama for his chapel in Santa Maria Novella, it flatters the Medici: Vasari identified Cosimo the Elder as the oldest king, and other family members appear among the onlookers.
artworks.lookCloser: The young man in a golden-yellow cloak at far right, looking straight at us, is generally accepted as Botticelli's self-portrait.

artworks.title: La Velata (Woman with a Veil)
artworks.blurb: A young woman in a white veil turns toward us with one hand on her breast, her sleeve a great cascade of gold and ivory silk. Raphael gave the fabric as much attention as the face. She is traditionally identified as Margherita Luti, the Roman baker's daughter said to be his mistress, and the same model seems to appear in his Fornarina.
artworks.lookCloser: Follow the folds of the enormous sleeve, painted with quick, sure strokes, then compare its busy surface with the calm, smooth modelling of her face.

artworks.title: The Second of May 1808
artworks.blurb: Madrileños armed with knives attack the Mameluke cavalry of Napoleon's Imperial Guard near the Puerta del Sol, in a tangle of horses, turbans and blood. Goya painted it in 1814 with its companion, The Third of May, after the French had been driven out of Spain. There is no single hero or focal point, only chaos.
artworks.lookCloser: At the centre a townsman drags a wounded Mameluke from his white horse. The canvas was badly torn in a truck accident in 1936 and restored again in 2007–08.

artworks.title: The Alchemist Discovering Phosphorus
artworks.collection: Derby Museum and Art Gallery, Derby
artworks.blurb: In a vaulted, church-like laboratory, an old alchemist kneels in wonder before a flask blazing with white light. Wright's full title says he was seeking the philosopher's stone and found phosphorus instead, a discovery made by Hennig Brand of Hamburg in 1669 by boiling down urine. Chemistry here borrows the look of a religious vision.
artworks.lookCloser: Two assistants at the left are lit by warmer candlelight, and a full moon shows through the Gothic window, possibly a nod to Wright's friends in the Lunar Society.

artworks.title: The Three Graces
artworks.blurb: Three nude Graces stand close together before a soft, open landscape, each holding a golden sphere. Barely 17 centimetres square, the panel is the young Raphael's first known treatment of the female nude seen from front and back, often linked to an ancient marble group in Siena Cathedral. It may once have been paired with his Vision of a Knight.
artworks.lookCloser: The central Grace turns her back to us while her sisters face forward. Their golden spheres have been read as the apples of the Hesperides.

artworks.title: Portrait of a Young Girl
artworks.blurb: A young woman in a truncated hennin and an ermine-trimmed gown looks sidelong out of a plain wainscoted room. Petrus Christus, working in Bruges in the wake of Jan van Eyck, sets her in a real space lit from the left, and gives her an alert, reserved gaze that few sitters of the time turn on the viewer.
artworks.lookCloser: Her eyes are slightly misaligned and her eyebrows faintly skewed, which sharpens her stare. Note the black band under her chin, a detail rarely seen in portraits of the period.

artworks.title: Lion Capital of Ashoka
artworks.blurb: Four lions sit back to back on this capital, which once crowned a column raised by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka at Sarnath, where the Buddha preached his first sermon. Carved from a single block of sandstone and polished to a glassy sheen, it was excavated in 1904–05. It is the model for India's state emblem, and its wheel sits at the centre of the national flag.
artworks.lookCloser: Around the drum below the lions, an elephant, a bull, a galloping horse and a lion walk between spoked wheels, all moving from right to left.

artworks.title: Venus de' Medici
artworks.blurb: Aphrodite, goddess of love, is caught as if surprised on emerging from the sea, shielding her body with her arms. This 1st-century BCE marble copies a lost Greek bronze in the tradition of Praxiteles' Aphrodite of Knidos. Sent from Rome to the Uffizi's Tribuna in 1677, it became a high point of the Grand Tour.
artworks.lookCloser: The dolphin at her feet alludes to her birth from the sea. The long, tapering fingers come from a 17th-century restoration by Ercole Ferrata, and the signature on the base is a later addition.

artworks.title: Hermes and the Infant Dionysus
artworks.blurb: Hermes leans against a tree trunk draped with his cloak, holding the infant god Dionysus on his left arm. The group was found in 1877 in the ruins of the Temple of Hera at Olympia, where the traveller Pausanias had seen a Hermes by Praxiteles. Whether this is that original or a later work is still fiercely debated.
artworks.lookCloser: Hermes' face and chest are polished to a soft glow, while his back still shows rasp and chisel marks. His surviving sandal kept traces of red cinnabar and gilding.

artworks.title: The Harvesters
artworks.collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
artworks.blurb: Peasants scythe and bind golden wheat under a hot late-summer sky, while others break under a tree for bread, cheese and pears. Painted for the Antwerp banker Nicolaes Jonghelinck, it belongs to a cycle of the times of the year, five of which survive. The Met calls it the first modern landscape.
artworks.lookCloser: Beyond the fields, villagers play the cruel game of cock-throwing, figures bathe in a pond and ships sit on the distant water. At far right, someone climbs a tree to pick fruit.

artworks.title: Flaming June
artworks.collection: Museo de Arte de Ponce, Ponce
artworks.blurb: A woman in a sheer orange gown sleeps curled on a marble bench, with a sunlit sea glittering behind her. Frederic Leighton first designed the figure as a detail in another picture, then gave her this square canvas of her own. Long out of fashion, it resurfaced in London in the 1960s and was bought for the Museo de Arte de Ponce in Puerto Rico.
artworks.lookCloser: The sprig of oleander at top right is poisonous, possibly a hint at the thin line between sleep and death. Her pose loosely recalls Michelangelo's statue of Night.

artworks.title: Madonna with the Long Neck
artworks.blurb: The Virgin, impossibly tall and elegant, balances an oversized Christ Child on her lap while six angels crowd into the left side of the picture. Begun in 1534 for a funerary chapel in Parma, it was still unfinished when Parmigianino died in 1540. Its stretched proportions and lopsided space make it a textbook case of Mannerism.
artworks.lookCloser: Far below at right, a tiny St Jerome stands by a row of columns, barely reaching the Virgin's knee. The vase held by one angel shows the faint image of a cross.

artworks.title: Alba Madonna
artworks.medium: Oil on panel, transferred to canvas
artworks.blurb: Seated on the ground in an open Italian landscape, the Virgin watches as the infant John the Baptist offers a slender cross to the Christ Child, who grasps it, accepting his future Passion. Raphael fits the pyramid of figures into a round panel with ease. The Soviet government secretly sold it from the Hermitage to Andrew Mellon in 1931.
artworks.lookCloser: The flowers at the Virgin's feet carry meaning: violets for humility, cyclamen for love and sorrow, and red-centred anemones for the Passion.

artworks.title: Garden at Sainte-Adresse
artworks.collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
artworks.blurb: On a flowering terrace above the Channel near Le Havre, members of Monet's family take the sun while sailboats and steamers pass. Painted in the summer of 1867, it pairs smooth passages with quick, separate strokes of pure colour. The high viewpoint and stacked bands of terrace, sea and sky echo the Japanese prints Monet collected.
artworks.lookCloser: Monet called it "the Chinese painting in which there are flags." Two flags snap in the same sea breeze, one of them the French tricolour.

artworks.title: Washington Crossing the Delaware
artworks.collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
artworks.blurb: George Washington stands in a crowded boat pushing through ice on the Delaware on the night of 25–26 December 1776, the crossing that led to victory at Trenton. Emanuel Leutze painted it in Düsseldorf, hoping America's revolution would encourage Europe's reformers after 1848. The first version was destroyed in Bremen in 1942; this full-size replica has been at the Met since 1897.
artworks.lookCloser: The Stars and Stripes held by James Monroe did not exist until 1777. The river behind is modelled on the Rhine, not the Delaware.

artworks.title: The Last Judgment
artworks.medium: Oil and tempera on oak panel
artworks.blurb: Christ sits in judgement on a rainbow while St Michael, in gleaming armour, weighs souls below: the saved climb to a Gothic gate of heaven at left, the damned tumble into fire at right. Hans Memling painted it in Bruges for Angelo Tani, the Medici agent there. Bound for Florence, it was seized at sea by a Danzig privateer and never reached Italy.
artworks.lookCloser: The kneeling soul in one pan of St Michael's scales has the face of the banker Tommaso Portinari, painted on a separate piece of foil and glued in later.

artworks.title: The Elevation of the Cross
artworks.blurb: Nine straining men heave upright the cross to which Christ is already nailed, a great diagonal of muscle and effort that spills onto both wings. Rubens painted the triptych for the high altar of St Walburga's church in Antwerp soon after returning from Italy. It brought large-scale Baroque painting to Flanders and made his name.
artworks.lookCloser: In the left wing, St John quietly holds the Virgin's hands while the women below recoil in horror. A panting dog bursts into the lower left corner of the centre panel.

artworks.title: Dante and Virgil in Hell
artworks.blurb: In the circle of Hell reserved for falsifiers, Dante and his guide Virgil look on as two damned souls fight without end: the impostor Gianni Schicchi sinks his teeth into the neck of the alchemist Capocchio. The young William-Adolphe Bouguereau showed this muscular, lurid scene from Dante's Inferno at the Salon of 1850.
artworks.lookCloser: Above the fighters a bat-winged demon hovers with folded arms, grinning at the spectacle. Behind, more of the damned writhe in the smoky dark.

artworks.title: The Swing
artworks.blurb: A young woman in a white dress with blue bows stands on a swing in a Montmartre garden, half listening to a man seen from behind, while a small girl gazes up at them. Renoir scatters patches of pale colour over clothes and ground to catch sunlight filtering through leaves. His fellow painter Gustave Caillebotte bought it in 1877.
artworks.lookCloser: Look at the dabs of light on the man's jacket and the path. Critics in 1877 mocked them as looking like grease stains.

artworks.title: The Temptation of Saint Anthony
artworks.collection: Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga, Lisbon
artworks.blurb: Across three panels the hermit Anthony is carried aloft by demons, collapses after his fall, and finally kneels calm amid a black mass of monsters, false priests and hybrid creatures, with a burning village beyond. Bosch drew on the Life of St Anthony and the Golden Legend, and his inventions were copied for decades. Tree-ring dating places it around 1501.
artworks.lookCloser: At the centre Anthony looks straight out at us and points towards a tiny Christ standing by a crucifix in the dark ruined tower.

artworks.title: Venus, Cupid, Folly and Time
artworks.blurb: Venus and her son Cupid kiss in a cold, crowded foreground, watched by a boy about to throw roses, usually read as Folly, and by bald Father Time, who sweeps back a blue curtain. Probably the Bronzino that Vasari says was sent to Francis I of France, it mixes eroticism with warnings about love. What every figure means is still disputed.
artworks.lookCloser: Folly's right foot is pierced by a thorn, yet he keeps smiling. Venus holds the golden apple she won at the Judgement of Paris.

artworks.title: Danaë
artworks.blurb: Danaë, shut away in a bronze tower by her father, is visited by Zeus in the form of a shower of gold. Klimt packs her curled, sleeping body into an almost square canvas, wrapped in a sheer purple veil, with the golden stream pouring between her thighs. Painted at the height of his golden phase, it turns myth into erotic ornament.
artworks.lookCloser: Among the falling coin-like discs of gold sits one upright black rectangle, a sharp geometric note against the curves of her body.

artworks.title: Madonna del Granduca
artworks.blurb: The Virgin stands against a dark ground, holding the Christ Child and looking gently down and away. Raphael painted it around 1505, soon after arriving in Florence, and the soft sfumato modelling shows what he had learned from Leonardo. It takes its name from Ferdinand III, Grand Duke of Tuscany, who owned it.
artworks.lookCloser: The black background is a later addition. X-rays show that Raphael first painted an interior with an arched window and a glimpse of countryside.

artworks.title: The Large Bathers
artworks.blurb: Female nudes gather on a riverbank beneath trees that lean together to form a tall arch. Cézanne worked on this, the largest of his Bathers, for about seven years, and it was still unfinished at his death in 1906. Its blocky, simplified bodies, built like his landscapes and still lifes, pointed the way to Cubism.
artworks.lookCloser: The trunks on either side lean inward to form a great triangle, echoed by the poses of the bathers below. In places the pale ground shows through the thin paint.

artworks.title: The Seven Deadly Sins and the Four Last Things
artworks.blurb: Seven scenes of ordinary sin, from a brawl outside an inn to a family gorging at table, ring a great eye whose pupil shows Christ rising from the tomb above the words "Beware, beware, the Lord sees." Four roundels show Death, Judgement, Heaven and Hell. Philip II kept it in his bedroom; some scholars give it to a follower of Bosch.
artworks.lookCloser: In the scene of Pride, a woman admires her headdress in a mirror held up for her by a demon.

artworks.title: Woman with a Parrot
artworks.collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
artworks.blurb: A nude woman lies on her back on rumpled drapery, her long red hair spilling out, as a parrot alights on her raised hand. Courbet tuned the pose and smooth flesh to Salon taste, and in 1866 it became his first nude accepted there. Critics still objected to her tangled hair and cast-off clothes.
artworks.lookCloser: The parrot's empty perch stands behind her, so the bird has just flown down to her fingers. The model was probably Joanna Hiffernan, who posed often for Courbet.

artworks.title: Portrait of a Lady
artworks.blurb: A young woman in a black Burgundian gown turns three-quarters towards us, eyes lowered and fingers tightly clasped, a transparent veil spilling from her headdress. Against a flat blue-green ground, Rogier van der Weyden builds her from a few clean shapes: veil, neckline, face and hands. It is his only accepted portrait of a woman; her name is unknown.
artworks.lookCloser: Look for the pins pushed into the veil to hold it in place, and the bright red sash buckled beneath her breast.

artworks.title: Stele of the Vultures
artworks.blurb: Carved on both sides, this limestone slab celebrated King Eannatum of Lagash's victory over the neighbouring city of Umma. One face shows the god Ningirsu holding the enemy trapped in a great net; the other shows Eannatum leading a dense phalanx of shielded spearmen over the fallen. Found in fragments at Tello in southern Iraq, it is the earliest known war monument.
artworks.lookCloser: In the top register, vultures fly off with the severed heads of the enemy dead, the detail that gave the stele its name.

artworks.title: Venus Callipyge
artworks.blurb: A young woman lifts her light peplos to bare her hips and looks back over her shoulder, perhaps to admire them. This Roman marble copies a lost Greek bronze of about 300 BCE; whether she is Venus or a mortal is uncertain. Her famous backward glance is the work of restorers, since the head was missing when the statue was found.
artworks.lookCloser: Her head, arms and one leg are replacements by Carlo Albacini, who restored the statue in the 1780s before it went to Naples with the Farnese collection.

artworks.title: David
artworks.blurb: David twists at the instant before he lets fly the stone at Goliath, lips clamped, brow knotted, sling pulled taut. Carved in a matter of months in 1623–24 for Cardinal Scipione Borghese, it breaks with Michelangelo's poised, waiting David: this one launches into the space around it, making the viewer part of the action.
artworks.lookCloser: Bernini is said to have used his own face for David's bitten lip and frown. At his feet lie King Saul's discarded armour and a harp.

artworks.title: Farnese Hercules
artworks.blurb: Hercules, weary after his labours, leans heavily on his club, draped with the skin of the Nemean lion. This colossal marble, signed by the Athenian Glykon, was made for the Baths of Caracalla in Rome after a lost 4th-century BCE bronze by Lysippos or his circle. Dug up in 1546, it fixed the image of the hero for European art.
artworks.lookCloser: Walk round the back: in his right hand, hidden behind him, Hercules holds the golden apples of the Hesperides, the prize of one of his last labours.

artworks.title: The Lady and the Unicorn
artworks.blurb: In six tapestries woven in Flanders around 1500 from designs drawn in Paris, a noble lady stands on an island of flowers between a lion and a unicorn. Five are read as the senses: taste, hearing, sight, smell and touch. The sixth, inscribed "À mon seul désir", remains a puzzle. The banners bear the arms of the Le Viste family.
artworks.lookCloser: In Sight, the unicorn rests its front legs in the lady's lap and gazes at its own reflection in the mirror she holds up.

artworks.title: Isenheim Altarpiece
artworks.medium: Oil and tempera on limewood panels, with carved sculpture
artworks.blurb: Painted by Matthias Grünewald for the Antonite monks of Isenheim, who nursed sufferers of ergotism and other skin diseases, the closed altarpiece shows Christ's body grey-green, torn by thorns and covered in sores. Patients could see their own afflictions in his. Hinged wings open onto an Annunciation, a Nativity and a Resurrection, and then onto Nikolaus Hagenauer's carved shrine.
artworks.lookCloser: Christ's fingers splay and twist in agony against the black sky. At right, John the Baptist, long dead by then, points at him with an impossibly long finger.

artworks.title: Fine Wind, Clear Morning (Red Fuji)
artworks.medium: Woodblock print, ink and colour on paper
artworks.blurb: Mount Fuji fills the sheet, turned red by the morning sun in early autumn, when a southerly wind clears the sky. Hokusai reduces the scene to a few bands of colour: red slopes streaked with snow, a dark green forest at the base, and a blue sky rippled with rows of small clouds. It belongs to his Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji.
artworks.lookCloser: Early impressions are much paler, the rare "Pink Fuji"; later printings deepened the red and added a block of blue over the clouds at the horizon.

artworks.title: The Woman in the Waves
artworks.collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
artworks.blurb: A woman rises from the sea with her arms raised behind her head, the waves breaking around her body. Courbet, the leader of Realism, paints her as a flesh-and-blood bather rather than a goddess born from the foam, with ruddy skin and a trace of underarm hair. A small sailing ship sits on the horizon under an evening sky.
artworks.lookCloser: Note the trace of underarm hair, a realist touch that smooth academic nudes left out.

artworks.title: Young Girls at the Piano
artworks.blurb: Two girls lean together over an upright piano in a comfortable bourgeois room, one in white with a blue sash seated and playing, the other in pink standing to follow the music. Renoir painted this version in 1892 for the state's Musée du Luxembourg and made several others for dealers and collectors, changing poses and details each time.
artworks.lookCloser: Behind the girls, a heavy curtain and a vase of flowers on the piano set the domestic scene, handled in soft, feathery strokes.

artworks.title: Women in the Garden
artworks.blurb: Four women in fashionable summer dresses gather flowers in a sunlit garden at Ville-d'Avray. Monet painted the huge canvas outdoors, lowering it into a trench to reach the top, and his companion Camille Doncieux posed for the figures. The Salon rejected it in 1867, and his friend Frédéric Bazille bought it to help him out.
artworks.lookCloser: One biographer says the woman at right seems to glide along the path "as if she had a trolley concealed beneath her dress". Monet cared more about light than anatomy.

artworks.title: Tahitian Women on the Beach
artworks.blurb: Two Tahitian women sit close together yet apart, one in a flowered pareu, the other in a high-necked pink missionary dress, a sign of French colonial rule. Gauguin painted it during his first stay on Tahiti, using flat bands of ochre, green and blue. Whether they sit on a beach at all is debated: the bands may be architecture.
artworks.lookCloser: The women's faces are simplified almost into masks, and their heavy, sculptural bodies fill the canvas nearly edge to edge.

artworks.title: The Feast in the House of Levi
artworks.blurb: Christ sits at the centre of a vast banquet framed by three Roman arches, surrounded by servants, soldiers, dwarfs and dogs. Painted as a Last Supper for the refectory of Santi Giovanni e Paolo in Venice, it brought Paolo Veronese before the Inquisition in 1573 for its irreverent extras. Rather than repaint it, he changed the subject to Levi's feast.
artworks.lookCloser: The new subject is written on the stair balustrades, citing Luke, chapter 5. Nearby are the man with a nosebleed and the drunken German soldiers the inquisitors objected to.

artworks.title: Equestrian Portrait of Charles V
artworks.blurb: Emperor Charles V rides alone through an open landscape, lance in hand, after his 1547 victory over the Protestant forces at Mühlberg. Titian painted it at the imperial court in Augsburg in 1548, copying the actual armour and horse trappings, which survive in Madrid's Royal Armoury. Charles looks controlled and pensive rather than triumphant.
artworks.lookCloser: Titian sent to Venice for red lake pigment. Its crimson glows on the sash, the plume and the horse's trappings, the colour of the Catholic cause.

artworks.title: Portrait of Innocent X
artworks.blurb: Pope Innocent X sits in a red chair before a red curtain, in red cap and cape, fixing the viewer with a hard, wary look. Velázquez painted him in Rome around 1650, turning silk, linen and flushed skin into quick, sure strokes. Francis Bacon later reworked it in dozens of screaming popes.
artworks.lookCloser: The folded paper in the pope's hand carries Velázquez's signature; the date on it is no longer legible.

artworks.title: The Intervention of the Sabine Women
artworks.blurb: Hersilia, daughter of the Sabine leader Titus Tatius and wife of Rome's founder Romulus, flings herself between the two men with arms spread, as other women thrust their babies into the battle. Jacques-Louis David began planning it in prison in 1795, and it was read as a plea for reconciliation after the Terror. The warriors fight nude, like Greek statues.
artworks.lookCloser: Behind the battle rises the Tarpeian Rock, from which Roman traitors were thrown, a pointed reminder of civil strife.

artworks.title: Nymphs and Satyr
artworks.blurb: Surprised while bathing in a secluded pool, a ring of nymphs turns on the satyr who spied on them and tries to drag him into the cold water. William-Adolphe Bouguereau built the interlocking poses from careful studies of models and showed it at the 1873 Salon. It later hung in the bar of New York's Hoffman House Hotel.
artworks.lookCloser: One of the satyr's hooves is already in the water, and he is plainly resisting. More nymphs hang back in the shadows at right.

artworks.title: Flora
artworks.blurb: A young woman with loose golden hair and a slipping white chemise holds out a handful of flowers while clutching a pink mantle with her other hand. Titian painted this ideal Venetian beauty around 1515. Whether she is the goddess Flora, a bride or a courtesan is still disputed; the name comes only from her spring flowers.
artworks.lookCloser: The flowers in her right hand are the only clue to the title. Rembrandt knew the picture and borrowed from it for his Saskia as Flora.

artworks.title: The Haywain Triptych
artworks.blurb: A towering cart of hay, emblem of worldly goods, rolls towards Hell pulled by demons, while pope, emperor, monks and peasants scramble to grab at it or follow behind. On the left wing sin enters the world with the fall of the angels and of Adam and Eve; on the right, demons build Hell. Christ looks down from the clouds, unnoticed.
artworks.lookCloser: On top of the hay, a pair of lovers make music beside a praying angel and a blue demon who plays along. Only the angel looks up at Christ.

artworks.title: The Nightmare
artworks.blurb: A sleeping woman lies flung backwards across a bed while a squat, ape-like incubus crouches on her chest and a horse with pupil-less eyes pushes through the red curtains. Fuseli, a Swiss painter working in London, showed it at the Royal Academy in 1782, where its open eroticism shocked critics and made his name. Engravings soon spread it across Europe.
artworks.lookCloser: The horse is a visual pun on the word "nightmare". A preliminary chalk sketch has no horse, so Fuseli may have added it late.

artworks.title: Judith I
artworks.medium: Oil and gold leaf on canvas
artworks.blurb: Klimt turns the biblical widow who beheaded the Assyrian general Holofernes into a Viennese femme fatale. Judith, half-dressed in sheer fabric, looks down at us through lowered lids with parted lips, while Holofernes' head is pushed to the lower right and cut off by the edge. Gold leaf fills the background with stylised trees and locks her into a flat, shimmering surface.
artworks.lookCloser: There is no sword and no blood. Many viewers have seen in Judith's face the Viennese socialite Adele Bloch-Bauer, whom Klimt later painted twice.

artworks.title: The Torment of Saint Anthony
artworks.blurb: Demons covered in scales, spines and horns seize Saint Anthony in mid-air and try to drag him down, while the hermit stays calm. The panel copies an engraving by the German printmaker Martin Schongauer. The Kimbell attributes it to Michelangelo at about 12 or 13, which would make it his earliest known painting, though not every scholar accepts this.
artworks.lookCloser: His early biographer Condivi says the boy went to the fish market to study scales. He also added the landscape below, which is not in Schongauer's print.

artworks.title: Woman with a Parasol – Madame Monet and Her Son
artworks.blurb: Camille Monet stands on a rise in a meadow at Argenteuil, seen from below against a bright, cloud-streaked sky, while the wind tugs at her veil and white dress. Their seven-year-old son Jean stands further back, cut off at the waist by the slope. Painted outdoors in a few hours, it is a family moment rather than a formal portrait.
artworks.lookCloser: The green of the meadow reappears on the underside of the parasol. Monet signed and dated it "Claude Monet 75" at lower right.

artworks.title: Aristotle with a Bust of Homer
artworks.collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
artworks.blurb: A philosopher in a broad black hat and wide, gold-lit sleeves rests his hand on a bust of the blind poet Homer, his shadowed eyes lost in thought. Rembrandt painted it for the Sicilian collector Antonio Ruffo, who left the subject open. The sitter has been read as Aristotle since Julius Held's 1969 study, though other identities have been proposed.
artworks.lookCloser: The medallion on his heavy gold chain bears a portrait of Alexander the Great, Aristotle's pupil, one of the clues used to identify the sitter.

artworks.title: Old Woman Cooking Eggs
artworks.blurb: An old woman cooks eggs in an earthenware dish over a small stove while a boy arrives with a flask and a melon. Velázquez painted this bodegón, or kitchen scene, in Seville when he was about nineteen. Hard light from the left picks out the woman, her pots and the eggs, and leaves the boy and the wall behind in deep shadow.
artworks.lookCloser: Scholars still argue over whether she is frying or poaching the eggs. The same model appears in Velázquez's Christ in the House of Martha and Mary.

artworks.title: The Large Bathers
artworks.blurb: Nude women play at the edge of a stream: one standing in the water is about to splash a friend, who leans back to dodge it. Renoir spent three years and more than twenty studies on the picture after a trip to Italy turned him towards Raphael and Ingres. He traced the main figures from drawings and gave them crisp, sculptural outlines.
artworks.lookCloser: Compare the halves: the hard-edged bathers at left, traced from drawings, against the loosely brushed swimmers and landscape at right, painted in his earlier Impressionist manner.

artworks.title: The Lunch
artworks.blurb: Three men share a plain meal of bread, pomegranates and wine at a table spread with a creased white cloth. An old man sits at left, a young man grins at right, and a boy behind them pours the wine. It is one of Velázquez's earliest known paintings, made in Seville around the age of eighteen, and he painted a near-identical version, The Farmers' Lunch.
artworks.lookCloser: The young man at right raises his thumb. On the wall behind hang a white collar, a leather bag and a sword.

artworks.title: Hylas and the Nymphs
artworks.blurb: The Argonaut Hylas, sent to fetch water, bends over a pool where seven naked nymphs rise among lily pads to draw him in, never to return. Waterhouse gives the nymphs near-identical faces, perhaps from only two models, and keeps Hylas in shadowed profile. Manchester bought it from the artist in 1896, and its brief removal from display in 2018 caused an outcry.
artworks.lookCloser: One nymph grips his wrist, another tugs at his tunic and a third offers pearls in her open palm. Among the lilies is an early depiction of the yellow water lily.

artworks.title: Artemision Bronze
artworks.blurb: A bearded god, slightly over life-size, stands with his arms stretched wide, about to hurl a weapon that is now lost. Most scholars read him as Zeus with a thunderbolt, though some prefer Poseidon with a trident. Cast around 460 BCE in the Severe style, he was recovered from an ancient shipwreck off Cape Artemision, in northern Euboea, in 1926–28.
artworks.lookCloser: The empty eye sockets once held inlaid eyes, probably of bone. The eyebrows were inlaid with silver, and the lips and nipples with copper.

artworks.title: Bacchus
artworks.blurb: The wine god, drunk and unsteady, lifts a cup and stares at it with rolling eyes, his soft body tipping back on its rocky base. The young Michelangelo carved it in Rome for Cardinal Raffaele Riario, who rejected it; the banker Jacopo Galli bought it for his garden of antique fragments. Vasari saw in it both a youth's slenderness and a woman's roundness.
artworks.lookCloser: Behind his leg, a small satyr eats the grapes slipping from Bacchus's left hand. The hand holding the cup is a restoration of the early 1550s.

artworks.title: Lady of Elche
artworks.blurb: A woman's limestone bust wears a tall headdress, large wheel-shaped coils over each ear and heavy layered necklaces. Found in 1897 at La Alcudia near Elche, it is the best-known work of Iberian sculpture, made by the pre-Roman people of eastern Spain, who absorbed Greek and Punic influences. A cavity in the back suggests it once served as a funerary urn.
artworks.lookCloser: The hollow eyes once held inlays of glass paste, and faint traces of the original paint survive on the stone.
