artworks.title: Apoxyomenos
artworks.year: c. 330 BCE original; Roman copy c. 50 CE
artworks.medium: Marble (Roman copy of a bronze original)
artworks.collection: Museo Pio-Clementino, Vatican Museums, Vatican City
artworks.blurb: An athlete scrapes sweat, oil and dust from his outstretched arm with a curved strigil. This marble, found in Trastevere in 1849, is a Roman copy of a lost bronze by Lysippos, court sculptor to Alexander the Great. Its small head, about one-eighth of the body's height, and long limbs show the slimmer canon of proportion Lysippos introduced.
artworks.lookCloser: The outstretched arm reaches towards the viewer, inviting you to walk around him. Pliny says Tiberius moved the bronze original into his bedroom until theatre crowds demanded it back.

artworks.title: The Seated Scribe
artworks.medium: Painted limestone, eyes inlaid with rock crystal and magnesite
artworks.blurb: A cross-legged man sits with a half-unrolled papyrus across his lap, his right hand poised as if to write. His face is alert and individual, his body soft and well fed, a sign of comfortable status. Auguste Mariette found the statue at Saqqara in 1850; who he was is unknown, since his name was probably carved on a larger base that is now lost.
artworks.lookCloser: The eyes are polished rock crystal set in white magnesite and held by copper clips. The reed brush once in his right hand is missing.

artworks.title: The Battle of Alexander at Issus
artworks.blurb: Thousands of armoured soldiers clash beneath a vast world landscape of sea, mountains and curving horizon, as Alexander the Great routs the Persian king Darius at Issus in 333 BCE. Duke William IV of Bavaria commissioned it in 1528 for a series of history paintings. The armour is that of Altdorfer's own day, and the victory may allude to the Ottoman siege of Vienna in 1529.
artworks.lookCloser: Find Darius fleeing in his chariot, pursued by Alexander. Above, a setting sun and a crescent moon share the sky, and a tasselled tablet records the battle in Latin.

artworks.title: Gabrielle d'Estrées and One of Her Sisters
artworks.blurb: Two women sit side by side in a bath, revealed by parted curtains as if on a stage. One is Gabrielle d'Estrées, mistress of King Henry IV; her sister pinches her right nipple, while Gabrielle holds up a ring. Painted by an unknown artist of the School of Fontainebleau, the gesture is traditionally read as announcing her pregnancy with the king's child.
artworks.lookCloser: In the background a woman sews by the fireplace, perhaps preparing clothes for the coming baby. Above the fire hangs a painting of a male nude.

artworks.title: Christ Carrying the Cross
artworks.blurb: Christ's calm face, eyes closed, sits in a crush of leering, toothless and snarling heads that fill the panel edge to edge. There is no landscape and almost no bodies, only faces pressed together like caricatures of human wickedness. Long given to Bosch himself, it is now thought by many specialists, including the Bosch Research and Conservation Project, to be by a follower.
artworks.lookCloser: At lower left, Saint Veronica holds her veil, miraculously marked with the face of Christ, while the jeering crowd presses in around her.

artworks.title: The Umbrellas
artworks.blurb: A Paris street fills with umbrellas as rain begins or ends. At left, a milliner's assistant with no umbrella lifts her skirt and carries a hatbox; at right, a mother bends towards her daughters. Renoir painted it in two campaigns: the right side in 1881 with feathery Impressionist strokes, the left around 1885 in a harder, more classical style.
artworks.lookCloser: X-rays show that the woman at left, modelled by Suzanne Valadon, first wore a hat and a frilled dress. Renoir repainted her in plainer working clothes.

artworks.title: Syndics of the Drapers' Guild
artworks.blurb: Five sampling officials of the Amsterdam cloth guild look up from a table draped with a Persian-style rug, a bareheaded servant behind them, as if interrupted. Their unpaid job was to grade the quality of cloth. In his last great group portrait Rembrandt used a low viewpoint, because the canvas was to hang high on a wall of their guildhall, the Staalhof.
artworks.lookCloser: The man at far right was long thought to hold a bag of seals. Restoration in 1991 showed that he holds a pair of gloves.

artworks.title: The Flagellation of Christ
artworks.blurb: In a classical hall at the back, Christ is bound to a column and whipped while Pilate watches from his throne. In the foreground, three men stand talking in a sunlit street and pay no attention. Piero built the scene with exact linear perspective, and who the three men are, and why they dominate the picture, has been argued over for centuries.
artworks.lookCloser: The two scenes are lit from opposite sides. Piero signed it on the step beneath Pilate's seat: "the work of Piero of Borgo San Sepolcro".

artworks.title: The Valpinçon Bather
artworks.blurb: A seated nude turns her back to us on the edge of a bed, her hair bound in a patterned headscarf. Ingres painted it at 28 while a student at the French Academy in Rome, and it takes its name from a later owner. Her pale, smooth back seems to float against a heavy green curtain and crisp white linen, calm rather than openly erotic.
artworks.lookCloser: Ingres reused this figure 55 years later as the mandolin player in The Turkish Bath. Man Ray borrowed her back for his 1924 photograph Le Violon d'Ingres.

artworks.title: Madonna in the Church
artworks.blurb: The crowned Virgin, far too tall for the building, stands in the nave of a Gothic church holding the Christ Child, who grips the neckline of her red dress. Daylight streams through the windows and falls in two pools on the floor, a sign of her purity. The tiny panel was probably the left wing of a diptych whose other half is lost.
artworks.lookCloser: In a doorway at right, two angels sing from a book. Behind Mary, a statue of her holding the Child stands in a niche, echoing her pose.

artworks.title: Madonna with Canon Joris van der Paele
artworks.blurb: The elderly canon Joris van der Paele kneels in a white surplice before the Virgin and Child, presented by his name saint, George, in shining armour. Saint Donatian, patron of his church in Bruges, stands at left in rich vestments. Gravely ill, van der Paele commissioned the panel as his memorial, and van Eyck recorded every fold of his ageing face.
artworks.lookCloser: The canon holds his spectacles over his prayer book. In Saint George's shield, van Eyck painted a tiny reflection of himself at his easel.

artworks.title: Chalk Cliffs on Rügen
artworks.blurb: Three visitors in town clothes look out from the white chalk cliffs of Rügen over a pale, luminous sea, framed by two leaning trees. Friedrich painted it after his 1818 honeymoon trip to the island. The woman in red is usually taken as his wife Caroline, and the man crouching on the grass beside his hat, peering over the edge, as the painter himself.
artworks.lookCloser: Two tiny sailing boats float far out on the sea. The figures' clothes, red, blue and green, have been read as love, faith and hope.

artworks.title: The Last Supper
artworks.blurb: Tintoretto sets the Last Supper in a dim Venetian inn, with the table running away from us on a steep diagonal. Servants clear dishes and a woman carries a plate in the foreground, while Christ gives bread to an apostle, his halo blazing. Painted in the artist's last years for the church of San Giorgio Maggiore, it points towards Baroque drama.
artworks.lookCloser: Smoke from the hanging oil lamp turns into a swarm of translucent angels that drift across the ceiling.

artworks.title: The Feast of the Gods
artworks.blurb: Gods, satyrs and nymphs drink and doze at a woodland picnic taken from Ovid. At right, Priapus lifts the dress of the sleeping nymph Lotis, and the bray of Silenus's ass at left will soon wake her. Giovanni Bellini signed it in 1514 for Duke Alfonso d'Este of Ferrara; Dosso Dossi and then Titian later repainted the landscape to match their pictures for the same room.
artworks.lookCloser: Bellini's signature and the date are written on a painted slip of paper stuck to the wooden tub at lower right. Blue-and-white Chinese porcelain bowls hold the fruit.

artworks.title: Franks Casket
artworks.blurb: This small box of whale bone is carved in low relief with scenes that mix Germanic legend, Roman history and Christian story: the smith Weland taking revenge, Romulus and Remus with the wolf, the Adoration of the Magi, the Roman capture of Jerusalem. Probably made in a Northumbrian monastery, it is framed with inscriptions mostly in Old English runes.
artworks.lookCloser: The runes around the front panel form a riddle about the casket's own material, a great fish beached on the shingle. Some inscriptions run upside down or backwards.

artworks.title: Farnese Bull
artworks.year: Roman copy, early 3rd century CE, of a 2nd-century BCE original
artworks.blurb: The brothers Amphion and Zethus tie Queen Dirce to a rearing bull to punish her cruelty to their mother, Antiope. The largest single sculpture yet recovered from antiquity, it was dug up in 1546 in the Baths of Caracalla in Rome for the Farnese family. It is usually seen as a Roman version of a Hellenistic group that Pliny credits to Apollonius and Tauriskos of Tralles.
artworks.lookCloser: The seated boy, the dog and other animals around the base may not belong to the original design: the group has been heavily restored since the 16th century.

artworks.title: Diana of Versailles
artworks.blurb: The huntress goddess strides forward in a short tunic, turning her head as she reaches over her shoulder for an arrow, a small deer leaping at her side. She is a Roman marble copy of a lost Greek bronze of about 325 BCE, often attributed to Leochares. Pope Paul IV gave her to Henry II of France in 1556, and she later stood in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.
artworks.lookCloser: Her left arm is a restoration, and the fragment in her hand may be part of a bow. Her second toes are longer than her big toes.

artworks.title: Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss
artworks.blurb: Cupid alights beside Psyche, who lies in the deathlike sleep released from the jar she was told not to open, and cradles her head as she reaches up to him. Their lips almost meet in the moment before the kiss. Colonel John Campbell commissioned it in 1787, and Canova set polished skin against rough rock and soft drapery.
artworks.lookCloser: The jar and the arrow lie on the rock behind Psyche. A handle near her foot let the sculpture be turned on its base, so it could be seen from every side.

artworks.title: The Fifer
artworks.blurb: A boy fifer from the band of Napoleon III's Imperial Guard, in red trousers, black jacket and white gaiters, stands against a plain, pale ground with no visible floor or wall. Manet painted him after seeing Velázquez's portraits in Madrid in 1865. The Salon jury rejected it in 1866, and Émile Zola defended him in print.
artworks.lookCloser: The black of the jacket and shoes is laid on thickly. Some have seen the features of Léon Leenhoff or of Victorine Meurent, Manet's favourite model, in the boy's face.

artworks.title: La Loge
artworks.blurb: A young woman in a black-and-white striped gown, pearls and pink roses sits at the front of a theatre box, while her companion looks up through opera glasses at someone else in the house. The models were Nini Lopez and Renoir's brother Edmond. Renoir showed it at the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874: the box was a place to see and be seen.
artworks.lookCloser: Her black stripes are mixed with blue, and the white ones hold touches of blue, green and yellow. X-rays suggest she first wore a hat.

artworks.title: The Triumph of Bacchus
artworks.blurb: Bacchus, pale and half-naked, places a wreath on a kneeling young man while a group of weathered Spanish peasants gathers to drink. Velázquez painted it for Philip IV, who paid 100 ducats, just before his first trip to Italy. Setting a classical god among street drinkers turns myth into something close to a tavern scene; in Spain it is known as Los borrachos, The Drunks.
artworks.lookCloser: At the god's feet, a bottle and an earthenware jug form a small still life, like those in Velázquez's early Seville kitchen scenes.

artworks.title: Apollo in the Forge of Vulcan
artworks.blurb: Apollo, crowned with laurel and glowing in an orange robe, steps into Vulcan's smithy to tell him that his wife Venus is sleeping with Mars. Vulcan and his muscular assistants freeze mid-work, stunned. Velázquez painted it in Rome during his first Italian journey, turning a story from Ovid into a scene of ordinary working men caught in a moment of shock.
artworks.lookCloser: The armour being forged is for Mars himself. Velázquez paints the steel breastplate, the anvil and the red-hot iron with almost photographic precision.

artworks.title: The Roses of Heliogabalus
artworks.blurb: The young Roman emperor Elagabalus watches from a raised couch as his guests below are buried under drifts of pink rose petals released from a false ceiling. In the unreliable Augustan History, the source of the story, some guests are smothered to death. Alma-Tadema reportedly had fresh petals sent from the south of France each week during the four months he spent on the canvas.
artworks.lookCloser: Behind the banquet, a woman in a leopard skin plays the double pipes beside a bronze Dionysus modelled on the Ludovisi Dionysus.

artworks.title: Two Sisters (On the Terrace)
artworks.blurb: A young woman and a small girl sit on the terrace of the Maison Fournaise restaurant at Chatou, with shrubs and the river Seine beyond the railing. The "sisters" were not related: the elder was modelled by Jeanne Darlot, an 18-year-old future actress. Renoir sold it to the dealer Durand-Ruel within months and showed it at the seventh Impressionist exhibition in 1882.
artworks.lookCloser: Look for the small basket of wool balls in the foreground. Renoir had just painted Luncheon of the Boating Party on the same terrace.

artworks.title: The Rape of the Daughters of Leucippus
artworks.blurb: The twins Castor and Pollux seize Phoebe and Hilaeira, daughters of King Leucippus, and haul them up towards their horses. Four bodies and two horses twist into one tight, turning mass against a low landscape and open sky. Rubens painted the figures and the specialist Jan Wildens the landscape; the Elector Palatine Johann Wilhelm bought it in Antwerp in 1716.
artworks.lookCloser: Castor wears armour, Pollux the boxer is bare-chested. A putto steadies Castor's horse while Pollux's rears, and a putto's black wing hints at the twins' fate.

artworks.title: The Monk by the Sea
artworks.blurb: A tiny figure in a dark robe stands on a pale dune before a black sea and a sky that fills three-quarters of the canvas. There is no framing tree, no boat, no path into the picture. Shown at the Berlin Academy in 1810 beside The Abbey in the Oakwood, it unsettled critics, and King Frederick William III bought both paintings.
artworks.lookCloser: The small white flecks on the dark water are breaking waves, often mistaken for seagulls. Scientific study found that Friedrich painted two sailing ships on the horizon, then removed them.

artworks.title: Children's Games
artworks.blurb: Crowds of children take over a town square and its large civic building, rolling hoops, walking on stilts, riding hobby horses and staging mock tournaments. Scholars have identified some eighty to ninety different games. Bruegel treats their play with the same absorbed seriousness as adult business, perhaps a reminder that grown-up affairs look just as childish in the eyes of God.
artworks.lookCloser: Look for children inflating a pig's bladder as a balloon, and others swimming in the river at the upper left, where the town opens onto a landscape.

artworks.title: Jupiter and Io
artworks.blurb: The nymph Io, seen from behind, melts into the embrace of Jupiter, who has turned himself into a dark cloud to hide from his jealous wife Juno. Correggio painted it for Federico II Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, as one of a series on the loves of Jupiter. Her warm, solid body is set against the grey, smoky vapour of the god.
artworks.lookCloser: Find Jupiter's face, barely visible in the cloud as he kisses her, and his vaporous hand at her waist, which she pulls closer.

artworks.title: The Bellelli Family
artworks.blurb: Degas painted his aunt Laura, her husband Baron Gennaro Bellelli and their daughters Giovanna and Giulia after staying with them in Florence, where the baron lived in political exile. Laura stands in mourning black beside her girls, while her husband sits apart at his desk, half turned away. The young painter made an unhappy marriage the real subject of a family portrait.
artworks.lookCloser: Behind Laura hangs a framed portrait of her father, Hilaire Degas, the painter's grandfather, whose recent death explains the black dresses.

artworks.title: Adoration of the Magi
artworks.blurb: Frederick the Wise of Saxony commissioned this panel for the castle church at Wittenberg. Dürer sets the Virgin and Child among ruined arches and dresses the kings in jewelled finery, joining northern detail to Italian perspective, proportion and pure colour. The art historian Heinrich Wölfflin called it the first completely lucid painting in German art.
artworks.lookCloser: The long-haired middle king is usually read as a self-portrait of Dürer, and his AD monogram sits on a stone block in the foreground.

artworks.title: Battle of Grunwald
artworks.blurb: Nearly ten metres wide, Jan Matejko's canvas shows the victory of Poland and Lithuania over the Teutonic Order in 1410. Grand Duke Vytautas, in red, raises his sword at the centre while the Grand Master, Ulrich von Jungingen, in white, is cut down beside him. The Nazis hunted for the painting during the occupation; it survived hidden near Lublin.
artworks.lookCloser: Saint Stanislaus, patron of Poland, appears in the sky above the carnage, and King Władysław Jagiełło watches on horseback from the distance at top right.

artworks.title: The Disrobing of Christ
artworks.blurb: El Greco's first major commission in Spain, painted for the sacristy of Toledo Cathedral, shows Christ about to be stripped before the Crucifixion. His red robe blazes at the centre of a wall of crowded heads and lances, while his calm face turns upward. The cathedral objected to details and to the price, and El Greco had to go to arbitration.
artworks.lookCloser: At lower right a man in yellow bores a hole in the cross for the nails. At lower left stand the three Marys, whose presence the cathedral authorities disputed.

artworks.title: The Meeting (Bonjour, Monsieur Courbet)
artworks.blurb: On a sunlit road outside Montpellier, Courbet, with his painting gear strapped to his back, is greeted by his patron Alfred Bruyas, hat in hand, and Bruyas's servant Calas, who lowers his eyes. The composition borrows from popular prints of the Wandering Jew. Courbet casts the artist as a free traveller who meets the man who pays him on equal terms.
artworks.lookCloser: Courbet gave himself the brightest light and a jutting, upturned beard. The coach that supposedly brought him is a small shape on the road behind.

artworks.title: The Stone Breakers
artworks.blurb: Courbet saw two men breaking stones on a road near Maisières and asked them to pose in his studio. An old man and a boy, faces hidden or shaded, labour in ragged clothes at nearly life size. Attacked at the Salon of 1850 as unfit for high art but praised by Proudhon, the canvas was lost, probably destroyed, in 1945.
artworks.lookCloser: Notice the boy's torn shirt and the old man's patched clothes. Courbet wrote that he had rarely met so complete an expression of poverty.

artworks.title: Bathers at Asnières
artworks.blurb: Young men and boys rest and swim in the Seine on a hot summer day, with the factory chimneys of Clichy and a railway bridge behind them in the haze. Seurat, aged 24, planned the huge canvas through many studies and built it from cross-hatched strokes of carefully chosen colour. The Salon jury rejected it in 1884.
artworks.lookCloser: Around 1887 Seurat went back to the canvas and added dots of orange, yellow and blue to the hat of the boy in the water, a sign of his new pointillist method.

artworks.title: The Railway
artworks.blurb: Victorine Meurent, the model for Olympia, sits with a book and a sleeping puppy by the iron railings above the tracks of the Gare Saint-Lazare, while a girl in white turns her back to watch the trains. Only a cloud of steam shows the railway itself. Visitors to the 1874 Salon found the subject baffling and the handling sketchy.
artworks.lookCloser: A bunch of grapes rests on the parapet at right, and behind the steam stands the building on the rue de Saint-Pétersbourg where Manet had his studio.

artworks.title: Moonlit Night on the Dnieper
artworks.blurb: A full moon breaks through the clouds and lays a path of greenish light across the river Dnieper, above dark banks and a sky that fills most of the canvas. Arkhip Kuindzhi showed it alone in a darkened hall in Saint Petersburg, lit by a single lamp, and crowds queued to see it. Some visitors looked for a light hidden behind the canvas.
artworks.lookCloser: The horizon sits very low, and the only bright notes are the moon and its reflection. Everything else is built from dark, closely related tones.

artworks.title: Carnation, Lily, Lily, Rose
artworks.blurb: Two girls in white light paper lanterns in a Cotswold garden of lilies, roses and carnations as day fades. They are Dolly and Polly Barnard, daughters of the illustrator Frederick Barnard. Sargent painted outdoors in the few minutes of dusk light each evening, over two summers at Broadway, and the Tate bought the picture in 1887 through the Chantrey Bequest.
artworks.lookCloser: The title comes from the refrain of a popular song. When the real flowers died in autumn, Sargent carried on painting with artificial ones.

artworks.title: Mr and Mrs Andrews
artworks.blurb: The newly married Robert and Frances Andrews pose under an oak at the edge of their Suffolk estate, he with gun and dog, she seated in pale blue silk. Thomas Gainsborough, then about 23, gave the wheat fields and open view almost as much room as the sitters. Once loved for its charm, it is now also read as a portrait of property.
artworks.lookCloser: Mrs Andrews's lap was left as bare canvas. It has been suggested that it was meant to hold a game bird, a book or a future child.

artworks.title: Indian Widow
artworks.collection: Derby Museum and Art Gallery, Derby
artworks.blurb: A Native American widow sits beneath a tree hung with her dead husband's weapons, keeping vigil while a storm gathers and a volcano smokes behind her. Joseph Wright of Derby gave her classical drapery but painted her headband, quilled cords and buffalo robe from authentic objects. It was shown at his solo exhibition in London in 1785, possibly the first in England.
artworks.lookCloser: The buffalo robe is decorated on its skin side, one of several details showing that Wright worked from genuine objects from as far west as the upper Great Lakes.

artworks.title: Echo and Narcissus
artworks.blurb: Waterhouse follows Ovid: the youth Narcissus lies on the bank, lost in his own reflection, while the nymph Echo, who can only repeat the words of others, watches him hopelessly from across the stream. Neither looks at the other. The Walker Art Gallery bought the painting in 1903, the year it was shown at the Royal Academy.
artworks.lookCloser: White narcissus flowers already grow beside the youth's foot, foretelling his fate, and a yellow water lily floats in the pool.

artworks.title: Dawn
artworks.collection: Birmingham Museum of Art, Birmingham, Alabama
artworks.blurb: A nude figure personifying the dawn floats above a pond of water lilies, a sheer scarf drifting around her, and reaches for the trumpet of a tall calla lily. It was the first of William-Adolphe Bouguereau's four Times of Day, followed by Dusk, Night and Day. Its flawless, polished finish is typical of the Salon painting the Impressionists reacted against.
artworks.lookCloser: The water lilies below close at night, and the calla lily was an old symbol of rebirth: fitting flowers for an allegory of the new day.

artworks.title: They Did Not Expect Him
artworks.blurb: A political exile, gaunt and shabby, walks unannounced into his family's sitting room. His mother rises from her chair, his wife turns from the piano, the boy looks up in hesitant joy and the little girl does not know him. Ilya Repin reworked the man's face several times after Pavel Tretyakov had bought the canvas, searching for the right mix of doubt and endurance.
artworks.lookCloser: On the wall hang portraits of the poets Shevchenko and Nekrasov, a print of Steuben's Golgotha and a faint image of the assassinated Alexander II on his deathbed.

artworks.title: The Tortoise Trainer
artworks.blurb: An old man in an outdated red robe and turban, a ney flute in his hands and a drum on his back, tries to train five tortoises in a worn upper room of the Green Mosque in Bursa. They ignore him and eat the leaves. Osman Hamdi Bey may have given the man his own features, and the scene is often read as a satire on slow Ottoman reform.
artworks.lookCloser: Above the pointed window runs an inscription meaning "The healing of the hearts is meeting with the beloved."

artworks.title: Christ in the Wilderness
artworks.blurb: Christ sits alone on a rock in a stony desert at dawn, hands clasped tight, facing the temptation told in the Gospels. Ivan Kramskoi shows a tired man deep in thought rather than a triumphant saviour, in cold, pale colour. Shown at the second Peredvizhniki exhibition in 1873, it was bought by Pavel Tretyakov, and Kramskoi turned down the Academy professorship offered for it.
artworks.lookCloser: Christ's bare feet rest on sharp stones, and the horizon cuts the canvas almost exactly in half behind him.

artworks.title: Stańczyk
artworks.blurb: The court jester Stańczyk slumps alone in a dark room while a royal ball goes on in the bright hall behind him. A letter on the table reports the loss of Smolensk to Muscovy, and only the fool grasps what it means. Jan Matejko, aged 24, gave the jester his own face, and the painting made his name.
artworks.lookCloser: Through the open window a comet hangs near the dark outline of Wawel Cathedral, an omen of misfortune. The jester's bauble lies discarded on the floor.

artworks.title: Allegory of Prudence
artworks.blurb: Three human heads, old, mature and young, look left, forward and right above the heads of a wolf, a lion and a dog. The image joins the three ages of man to past, present and future. The faces have been identified as Titian, his son Orazio and his nephew Marco, though scholars dispute this, and Titian's workshop may have helped.
artworks.lookCloser: A faint Latin inscription above the heads says, in short: from the past, the present acts prudently, lest it spoil future action.

artworks.title: Diana and Actaeon
artworks.collection: National Gallery, London, and Scottish National Gallery, Edinburgh
artworks.blurb: The hunter Actaeon stumbles on the goddess Diana bathing with her nymphs in a ruined grotto; she will turn him into a stag, to be torn apart by his own hounds. Titian painted it for Philip II of Spain as one of his poesie, mythologies drawn from Ovid. The National Galleries of London and Scotland bought it together in 2009.
artworks.lookCloser: A stag's skull sits on the pillar above Diana, a hint of Actaeon's fate. Diana herself wears a small crescent moon in her hair.

artworks.title: The Angelus
artworks.blurb: At dusk in a potato field near Barbizon, a man and a woman stop work and bow their heads as a distant church bell rings the Angelus. Millet remembered his grandmother halting field work for the prayer. Reproduced in countless prints, it fetched a record price in 1889, when a bidding war between the Louvre and an American buyer stirred patriotic feeling in France.
artworks.lookCloser: The steeple on the horizon belongs to the church of Chailly-en-Bière. Salvador Dalí believed the basket hid a child's coffin, but an X-ray did not convince scholars.

artworks.title: Portinari Altarpiece
artworks.blurb: Tommaso Portinari, the Medici bank's agent in Bruges, ordered this triptych of the Adoration of the Shepherds from Hugo van der Goes for the church of Florence's hospital of Santa Maria Nuova. The wings show Portinari, his wife and children with their patron saints. Its rough, sharply observed shepherds impressed Florentine painters when it arrived in 1483.
artworks.lookCloser: In the foreground stand a sheaf of wheat and two vessels of flowers, including irises and columbines, each loaded with meaning about Christ's Passion and the Eucharist.

artworks.title: The Fallen Angel
artworks.blurb: Lucifer, cast out of heaven, lies naked on a rock with one arm half hiding his face, while the loyal angels stream across the sky above him. Alexandre Cabanel painted it in Rome at 24, as one of the works students at the Villa Medici had to send back to Paris. The handsome youth turns defeat into wounded, furious pride.
artworks.lookCloser: Look at the eyes above his arm: tears of rage stand in them. A thorny bramble trails behind his legs.

artworks.title: Salt Cellar (Saliera)
artworks.blurb: Benvenuto Cellini made this gold table piece for King Francis I of France, reworking a model first made for Cardinal Ippolito d'Este. Neptune, for the sea, and a female figure of Earth sit facing each other, legs interlaced, on an ebony base. It is the only surviving gold work securely by Cellini, and was stolen from the museum in 2003 and recovered in 2006.
artworks.lookCloser: Salt went in the little boat beside Neptune and pepper in the tiny temple beside Earth. Reclining figures of the winds and the times of day ride on the base.

artworks.title: Venus of Laussel
artworks.medium: Limestone relief with traces of red ochre
artworks.blurb: Carved into a limestone block in a rock shelter at Laussel in the Dordogne, a woman with heavy breasts, belly and hips raises a horn in one hand and rests the other on her stomach. She belongs to the Gravettian culture of about 25,000 years ago and was once coloured with red ochre. The block was found in 1911.
artworks.lookCloser: The horn bears thirteen notches, which some read as a count of lunar months or cycles in a year. Her faceless head turns towards it.

artworks.title: Farnese Atlas
artworks.blurb: The Titan Atlas, condemned by Zeus to carry the heavens, kneels under a great celestial globe. This Roman marble, probably copied from a Hellenistic original, is the oldest surviving statue of Atlas, and its globe is the oldest known picture of the classical constellations. It takes its name from Cardinal Alessandro Farnese, who acquired it in 1562.
artworks.lookCloser: The constellations are carved in low relief without any stars: look for Aries the ram, Cygnus the swan and Hercules. A claim that they follow Hipparchus's lost star catalogue remains contested.

artworks.title: Barberini Faun
artworks.blurb: A satyr sprawls asleep on a rock, legs thrown open and head fallen back, as if after drinking. The statue is a Hellenistic original or a fine Roman copy, found in the 1620s below Castel Sant'Angelo in Rome and heavily restored for the Barberini family. Its frank sensuality made it famous, and Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria bought it for his new sculpture museum.
artworks.lookCloser: A small tail at the base of his spine and the animal skin beneath him mark him as a satyr. His right leg is a later restoration.

artworks.title: Diadumenos
artworks.medium: Marble copy of a lost bronze
artworks.blurb: A young athlete, fresh from victory, raises both arms to tie the winner's ribbon around his head. Polykleitos cast the original in bronze in the late fifth century BCE, and it survives only in marble copies. This one, carved around 100 BCE, was found in a house on the island of Delos.
artworks.lookCloser: His weight rests on the right leg with the left knee relaxed, the balanced stance Polykleitos made a rule. A cloak and quiver on the tree stump hint at an archery victory.

artworks.title: Circe Offering the Cup to Ulysses
artworks.blurb: The sorceress Circe, enthroned and staring straight out, holds up a cup of potion in one hand and a wand in the other. The viewer stands where Ulysses stands: he appears only in the round mirror behind her, with his ship beyond. At her feet lies one of his crew, already turned into a pig in this scene from Homer's Odyssey.
artworks.lookCloser: A second transformed sailor, now a pig, peers out from behind the throne at left, and the mirror also shows the columns of her palace.

artworks.title: Dulle Griet (Mad Meg)
artworks.collection: Museum Mayer van den Bergh, Antwerp
artworks.blurb: A tall woman in a breastplate and metal cap strides towards the mouth of hell, sword in hand and arms full of loot, while behind her an army of housewives plunders a house. Bruegel fills the burning landscape with monsters in the manner of Bosch. The picture plays on a Flemish proverb and mocks greed and folly.
artworks.lookCloser: A knife hangs at her side and she wears a single mailed glove. Beside her, a monster in a helmet parodies her armour as it pulls up a drawbridge.

artworks.title: The Glass of Wine
artworks.blurb: A woman in red silk drains a glass of wine while a man in a dark cloak stands over her, jug in hand, ready to pour more. A cittern and songbooks lie on the chair. Vermeer took the theme from Pieter de Hooch but set it in a richer, lighter room, and it counts among his first fully mature interiors.
artworks.lookCloser: In the open stained-glass window, a small figure of Temperance holds a bridle, a quiet warning set against the couple's drinking.

artworks.title: The Blind Girl
artworks.collection: Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery, Birmingham
artworks.blurb: Two travelling beggar girls rest by the roadside after a storm, with the town of Winchelsea behind them. The elder, blind, holds a concertina and feels the sun on her face and a blade of grass under her fingers, while her sister turns to look at a double rainbow. Millais builds the picture around what one can see and the other cannot.
artworks.lookCloser: A tortoiseshell butterfly rests on the blind girl's shawl. Millais first painted both rainbows with their colours in the same order, then corrected the outer one.

artworks.title: The Last Judgement (Beaune Altarpiece)
artworks.blurb: Nicolas Rolin, chancellor of Burgundy, and his wife Guigone de Salins commissioned this polyptych from Rogier van der Weyden for the hospital they founded at Beaune. Christ sits on a rainbow above the archangel Michael, who weighs souls, while the dead rise and walk to the gate of heaven on one side and fall into hell on the other.
artworks.lookCloser: Beside Christ's head float a lily for the saved and a sword for the damned, each with its Latin sentence written in the air, the blessed in white letters and the damned in black.

artworks.title: Women Gladiators
artworks.blurb: Before a crowd of men behind a low wall, two women in Roman-style robes fight with sword and shield; one has fallen and the other lifts her arm for the final thrust. Jusepe de Ribera painted it in Naples for a cycle of ancient Roman scenes sent to Philip IV's Buen Retiro palace. It has also been linked to a duel said to have been fought in Naples in 1552.
artworks.lookCloser: The standing gladiator is shown in strict profile, like a figure on an ancient relief, and both women wear classical hairstyles.

artworks.title: The Opening of the Fifth Seal
artworks.collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
artworks.blurb: Saint John, towering at the left, flings up his arms as the naked souls of martyrs writhe and reach for the robes of salvation described in Revelation. El Greco painted it in his last years for a church outside Toledo and left it unfinished. The painter Ignacio Zuloaga later owned it and showed it to Picasso, and it is often linked with Les Demoiselles d'Avignon.
artworks.lookCloser: At least 175 cm was cut from the top of the canvas in a botched restoration in 1880, which is why Saint John now gestures towards nothing.

artworks.title: Pollice Verso
artworks.blurb: In the Colosseum, a victorious gladiator plants his foot on a fallen opponent and looks up at the crowd, where Vestal Virgins in white thrust their thumbs down. Jean-Léon Gérôme's picture fixed the popular idea that thumbs down meant death, though the real Roman gesture is not known. It later helped persuade Ridley Scott to make the film Gladiator.
artworks.lookCloser: The defeated net-fighter raises two fingers to beg for mercy. The victor's helmet and armour are based on gladiatorial gear excavated at Pompeii.

artworks.title: Napoleon I on His Imperial Throne
artworks.blurb: Ingres shows the new emperor head-on, like an icon, in his coronation robes: gold laurel wreath, ermine, purple velvet strewn with gold bees, the sceptre of Charlemagne in one hand and the hand of justice in the other. At the Salon of 1806 critics found it strange and compared its style to that of Jan van Eyck.
artworks.lookCloser: An imperial eagle spreads across the carpet at his feet, and in the top right corner a cut-off shield bears the arms of Italian states under the crown of Italy.

artworks.title: Young Ladies on the Banks of the Seine (Summer)
artworks.blurb: Two Parisian women lie in the grass under oak trees by the Seine on a summer day, one drowsing with half-closed eyes, the other gazing at the water with a bouquet in her hand. Courbet gave this idle, modern subject the scale of a history painting, and its frank sensuality caused a scandal at the Salon of 1857.
artworks.lookCloser: A straw hat trimmed with flowers lies at the foot of the tree on the right, and a boat moored at the bank holds another hat and some fabric.

artworks.title: Eleanor of Toledo with Her Son Giovanni
artworks.blurb: Eleanor of Toledo, the Spanish wife of Duke Cosimo I de' Medici, sits beside her young son Giovanni against a glowing blue ground. Bronzino renders her brocade gown, pearls and cool, unreadable face with enamel-like precision. The portrait advertises the wealth she brought to Florence and the heirs she gave the new Medici dynasty.
artworks.lookCloser: Her gown carries a pomegranate pattern in black velvet on a white ground, a design Florence's silk weavers were famous for and a symbol of fertility.

artworks.title: The Slave Market
artworks.blurb: In a sunlit courtyard, a buyer opens the mouth of a naked woman to inspect her teeth while the dealer and other captives wait. Jean-Léon Gérôme set the scene in an imagined North African or Middle Eastern market and painted it with meticulous finish. It is now a standard example of Orientalist painting and of the fantasies it offered European viewers.
artworks.lookCloser: In the shaded arcade behind, another group of buyers inspects a nude man.

artworks.title: Nu couché
artworks.blurb: A young woman lies across the full width of the canvas, her body cropped by the edges and pushed close to the viewer. Known in English as Red Nude, it belongs to the series of nudes Modigliani painted in 1917 for his dealer Léopold Zborowski, and probably hung in his only solo show that year, which the police closed. It restates Titian's reclining Venus in simplified modern contours.
artworks.lookCloser: Look for the underarm hair and her faint smile: small touches of frankness that stop the figure from reading as an idealised goddess.

artworks.title: Jacob's Dream
artworks.blurb: The shepherd Jacob sleeps on his side beside a tree, while the ladder of his dream appears behind him not as timber but as a diagonal band of golden light. Ribera, the Spanish painter who worked in Naples and was known for harsh tenebrist contrasts, here gives most of the canvas to a quiet, glowing sky. Its warm tones later led collectors to take it for a Murillo.
artworks.lookCloser: The angels on the ladder are barely there, small shapes dissolving into the haze. Ribera signed and dated the canvas, yet it was listed as a Murillo in Queen Isabel Farnese's collection.

artworks.title: The Wayfarer
artworks.blurb: A thin, ragged pedlar with a basket on his back glances back at a run-down inn, where a couple lingers in the doorway and a man relieves himself against the wall. Ahead lies a closed gate. Once part of a lost triptych with Bosch's Ship of Fools, the roundel is read either as a man choosing between vice and virtue or as the Prodigal Son.
artworks.lookCloser: He wears a shoe on one foot and a slipper on the other, and a small dog snaps at his leg. A cat's skin hangs from his basket.

artworks.title: Madonna of the Magnificat
artworks.blurb: Two angels hold a crown of gold filigree over the Virgin as she writes the Magnificat, her song of praise from Luke's Gospel, in a book held by kneeling angels. The Christ Child on her lap guides her hand and rests his own on a pomegranate, a sign of the Passion. The figures curve with the round frame, a tondo made for private devotion in Florence.
artworks.lookCloser: Mary writes on the right-hand page; the left carries part of the Benedictus, Zechariah's song. Behind the group, a window opens onto a calm, pale river landscape.

artworks.title: The Goldfinch
artworks.blurb: A life-size goldfinch perches on its feeder against a pale plaster wall, held by a fine chain around its leg. Fabritius, a former pupil of Rembrandt, painted it as a trompe-l'oeil, probably set into a window jamb or used as a cover for another picture. The same year he was killed in the Delft gunpowder explosion, and only a handful of his works survive.
artworks.lookCloser: Up close the feathers are a few quick strokes of yellow, grey and red; from a distance they cohere. The signature 'C fabritivs 1654' runs along the bottom.

artworks.title: Ain Sakhri Lovers
artworks.blurb: Two figures clasp each other face to face, pecked out of a single calcite cobble with a stone point about 11,000 years ago. Found in a cave near Bethlehem used by Natufian people, it is thought to be the oldest known depiction of a couple having sex. There are no faces, and the sex of each figure can only be presumed, but the intimacy of the pose is clear.
artworks.lookCloser: Turn it and it changes: as the artist Marc Quinn has noted, from other angles the same stone reads as a phallus, breasts or a vulva.

artworks.title: Sarcophagus of the Spouses
artworks.collection: Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia, Rome
artworks.blurb: A husband and wife recline side by side on a banqueting couch, propped on cushions, smiling with almond-shaped eyes, as equals at an eternal feast. Found in the Banditaccia necropolis at Caere, it probably held cremated remains. Lively upper bodies give way to flattened legs, a typically Etruscan contrast. Once brightly painted, it was fired in four pieces and then assembled.
artworks.lookCloser: Check the feet at the end of the couch: the husband is barefoot, while his wife wears pointed shoes, a distinctively Etruscan fashion.

artworks.title: Apollo of Veii
artworks.collection: Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia, Rome
artworks.blurb: Striding forward in a clinging tunic and short cloak, the god once stood about twelve metres up on the roof of the Portonaccio temple at Veii, disputing the golden-horned hind with Heracles. Life-size and fired in one piece, it is often attributed to Vulca, the only Etruscan artist known by name, or his workshop. Its discovery in 1916 changed how Etruscan art was valued.
artworks.lookCloser: Note the archaic smile and the long spiralling curls tied with a ribbon. The reddish-brown skin follows the convention for male figures in Greek and Etruscan art.

artworks.title: Belvedere Torso
artworks.blurb: Only the massive, twisting trunk and thighs survive of this seated male nude, signed by Apollonios, son of Nestor, of Athens, probably after an earlier Hellenistic statue. Long read as Heracles, it may show Ajax contemplating suicide, the Vatican's favoured reading. In Rome by the 1430s, it fascinated Michelangelo, whose Sistine prophets and Last Judgement figures borrow its turning bulk.
artworks.lookCloser: The skin he sits on was long taken for a lion's pelt; recent study suggests a panther. The sculptor's Greek signature is carved on the front of the base.

artworks.title: Borghese Gladiator
artworks.blurb: A nude warrior lunges forward, his raised left arm once bearing a shield against an attacker on horseback, his right drawn back to strike. Despite the name, he is no gladiator. Found at Anzio before 1611 and signed by Agasias of Ephesus, it became one of the most copied antiquities, a model of anatomy for artists, and went from the Borghese collection to Paris in 1807.
artworks.lookCloser: The signature, 'Agasias, son of Dositheos, of Ephesus, made it', is carved on the tree-trunk support. The right arm is a later restoration; sword and shield are lost.

artworks.title: Knight, Death and the Devil
artworks.blurb: An armoured knight rides steadily through a rocky gorge, ignoring Death, a rotting corpse on a pale horse holding up an hourglass, and a goat-horned devil behind him. With Melencolia I and Saint Jerome in His Study it forms Dürer's three master engravings. The knight is usually read as the Christian soldier holding to his faith, with the city on the hill as his goal.
artworks.lookCloser: A skull lies directly in the knight's path, and his dog runs alongside. The tablet at lower left carries Dürer's monogram and the date 'S. 1513'.

artworks.title: The Beauty of Durrës
artworks.blurb: A woman's head, turned in three-quarter view, glows against a black ground scattered with lilies, hyacinths and bellflowers. Set from unworked river pebbles in the later fourth century BCE, the elliptical floor lay in a private house in Epidamnos, now Durrës. Austro-Hungarian engineers uncovered it during the First World War, and it is the oldest important mosaic found in Albania.
artworks.lookCloser: A single small yellow and red pebble in her pupil gives the eye its gaze. Her auburn braids are set off from the black ground by a thin white outline.

artworks.title: Maestà
artworks.blurb: The Virgin sits enthroned with the Christ Child among rows of angels and saints, with Siena's four patron saints kneeling in front. Commissioned by the city in 1308, it was carried in procession to the cathedral in 1311 while the shops stayed shut. Painted on both sides, its back told Christ's life in dozens of small scenes. It was sawn apart in 1771.
artworks.lookCloser: Along the base of the throne Duccio lettered a prayer: 'Holy Mother of God, be thou the cause of peace for Siena and life to Duccio because he painted thee thus.'

artworks.title: Warka Vase
artworks.blurb: Carved in bands of low relief, this tall vessel from the Eanna temple precinct at Uruk climbs from water and crops, through rams and ewes and naked men carrying offerings, to a goddess, probably Inanna, receiving gifts at her shrine. It is among the earliest narrative reliefs anywhere. Looted from the Iraq Museum in 2003, it was returned in pieces and restored.
artworks.lookCloser: Behind the goddess stand two bundles of reeds with streaming banners, the emblem of her shrine. The vase had already broken in antiquity and was mended with copper bands.

artworks.title: Bacchus
artworks.medium: Oil on walnut panel, transferred to canvas
artworks.blurb: A young man with an animal skin at his waist sits in a wooded landscape, pointing off to one side while his other hand holds a staff and points to the earth. It began as Saint John the Baptist, painted in Leonardo's workshop and now attributed to Francesco Melzi, though other pupils have been proposed. Between 1683 and 1693 it was repainted as the wine god Bacchus.
artworks.lookCloser: The vine wreath, the leopard spots on the skin and the Bacchic thyrsus were all added in the late 1600s; the thyrsus was once John's long, cross-shaped staff.

artworks.title: Mérode Altarpiece
artworks.blurb: The Annunciation takes place in a tidy Flemish home: Mary reads, seated on the floor against a bench, as Gabriel kneels, and a lily stands in a jug on the table. On the left the donors kneel in a garden; on the right Joseph works in his carpenter's shop. Attributed to Robert Campin and his workshop, it is a founding work of northern oil painting.
artworks.lookCloser: A tiny Christ Child carrying a cross glides toward Mary on rays of light through the left window. Joseph has made a mousetrap, and another sits for sale on his window ledge.

artworks.title: The Dog
artworks.medium: Mixed media on plaster, transferred to canvas
artworks.blurb: Only a dog's head shows above a dark, sloping mass, gazing up into a vast field of dirty ochre. Goya painted it straight onto a wall of his house outside Madrid, the Quinta del Sordo, as one of the Black Paintings he made for himself in his seventies and never titled. Whether the dog is sinking, hiding or waiting is left open.
artworks.lookCloser: A faint dark shape hangs in the ochre above the dog, generally thought to be a trace of the earlier picture Goya painted over. The murals were moved to canvas in the 1870s.

artworks.title: Nana
artworks.blurb: A young woman in a white chemise, blue corset and silk stockings pauses at her mirror, powder puff in hand, and turns to look at us, while a man in evening dress waits on the sofa. The model was the courtesan Henriette Hauser. Rejected by the 1877 Salon as an affront to morality, it was shown instead in a shop window on the Boulevard des Capucines.
artworks.lookCloser: The client is cut off by the right edge, leaving little more than his top hat, cane and profile. Behind the sofa a wading bird appears in the Japanese-style decoration.

artworks.title: The Merry Drinker
artworks.blurb: A ruddy man in a tilted hat raises a glass of wine and gestures toward us mid-sentence, as if we had just joined his table. Hals built him from fast, open strokes over a tinted ground, catching a passing moment rather than a pose. Whether he is a portrait sitter or a stock 'merry drinker' type is still debated; the Rijksmuseum now calls him a militiaman.
artworks.lookCloser: The medal on his chest may show Prince Maurice of Orange. His glass is a berkemeyer, a Dutch wine glass with a wide conical bowl, and his open smile shows his teeth.

artworks.title: Annunciation with Saints Maxima and Ansanus
artworks.blurb: Gabriel kneels in a swirl of patterned cloak and offers an olive branch, while Mary recoils on her throne, drawing her mantle close and keeping her place in her book. The whole scene floats on gold. Signed in 1333 by Simone Martini and his brother-in-law Lippo Memmi for Siena Cathedral, it flanks the scene with Saint Ansanus and a female saint, perhaps Maxima or Margaret.
artworks.lookCloser: Gabriel's greeting, 'Ave gratia plena dominus tecum', is raised in the gold and runs from his lips toward Mary. A vase of lilies stands between them.

artworks.title: Ludovisi Throne
artworks.collection: Palazzo Altemps, Museo Nazionale Romano, Rome
artworks.blurb: On the main face a goddess, usually read as Aphrodite rising from the sea, lifts her arms as two attendants on a pebbled shore raise a cloth to veil her. Carved around 460 BCE, probably for a temple of Aphrodite at Locri in southern Italy, the block was found in Rome in 1887. Its subject, purpose and even its authenticity have all been debated.
artworks.lookCloser: On the sides, turned away from the central scene, a nude girl plays the double flute and a veiled woman offers incense. Note how the goddess's wet drapery clings to her body.

artworks.title: Kritios Boy
artworks.blurb: A nude youth stands with his weight on one leg, the other knee slightly bent, so that hips, spine and shoulders shift in response. It is the earliest surviving statue to show this relaxed stance, contrapposto, and marks the break from the stiff archaic kouros. Found in the Persian debris on the Acropolis, it is attributed, on slender evidence, to the sculptor Kritios.
artworks.lookCloser: Compare the face with earlier kouroi: the archaic smile has gone, replaced by a grave, level expression. The torso was found in 1865, the head twenty-three years later.

artworks.title: Portrait of a Man (Self Portrait?)
artworks.blurb: A middle-aged man with stubbled cheeks and slightly bloodshot eyes turns to meet our gaze beneath a towering red headdress, painted fold by fold. The direct look and the prominent motto on the original frame have long suggested that van Eyck painted himself. The headdress is not a turban but a chaperon, its hanging sash wound up over the top.
artworks.lookCloser: The top of the frame bears his motto 'Als Ich Can' (As I can), a pun on his name. The bottom records that Jan van Eyck made it on 21 October 1433.

artworks.title: Olmec Colossal Heads
artworks.blurb: Seventeen of these heads are known, carved from basalt boulders brought more than 150 kilometres from the Tuxtla Mountains to Olmec centres on Mexico's Gulf Coast. Each has broad features, a heavy brow and its own close-fitting headdress, which is why they are thought to portray individual rulers. The head shown stands in Villahermosa; the others are divided among Mexican museums.
artworks.lookCloser: The headgear may represent protective helmets, perhaps for war or the ritual ballgame. The backs are often flat, and two heads were recarved from massive stone thrones.

artworks.title: Gebel el-Arak Knife
artworks.blurb: A rippled flint blade is set in an ivory handle carved on both faces in tiny relief. One side shows fighting men and boats; the other, a hunter in Mesopotamian-style robe and cap grasping two rearing lions. Made in late Predynastic Egypt and probably found at Abydos, it records contact with Mesopotamia shortly before the first pharaohs.
artworks.lookCloser: Look at the blade: long, even ripples of pressure flaking run across one face, while the other was left smoothly polished, perhaps to imitate metal.

artworks.title: Hamzanama
artworks.blurb: For the young emperor Akbar, a workshop led first by Mir Sayyid Ali and then Abd al-Samad illustrated the fantastical adventures of Amir Hamza, uncle of the Prophet, in some 1,400 large paintings on cotton, with the text on the back. It took about fifteen years. Only just over a hundred pages survive, among them this scene of the prophet Elijah rescuing Prince Nur ad-Dahr.
artworks.lookCloser: Elijah strides across the water to pull the drowning prince from a river full of fish and sea creatures, below a dense, layered forest.

artworks.title: Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains
artworks.blurb: Low hills, pines, riverbanks and villages unroll along more than six metres of paper in dry, layered strokes and pale ink washes. Huang Gongwang worked on the scroll for several years, around the age of eighty, near the Fuchun River. In 1650 a dying owner had it thrown on the fire; it survived in two pieces, reunited only briefly in 2011.
artworks.lookCloser: At the end of the scroll Huang's own inscription dedicates it to his Daoist friend Wuyong. Four centuries later the Qianlong Emperor dismissed this original as a fake.

artworks.title: Night-Shining White
artworks.collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
artworks.blurb: One of Emperor Xuanzong's horses strains against a tethering post, nostrils flared and eyes rolling, its round body drawn in taut ink lines with light shading and no colour. Han Gan, who claimed the imperial stables were his teachers, made it around 750. The small picture was later mounted on a long scroll to hold the seals and comments of twelve centuries of owners.
artworks.lookCloser: Among the seals and inscriptions crowding the paper are marks of the Southern Tang ruler Li Yu, the Song critic Mi Fu and the Qianlong Emperor.

artworks.title: Ardabil Carpet
artworks.medium: Wool pile on silk warps and wefts
artworks.blurb: A yellow central medallion ringed with pointed pendants floats on a deep blue field of scrolling tendrils and blossoms, with a mosque lamp hanging from each end of the medallion. Woven with about 26 million knots under Shah Tahmasp, it is thought to carry the earliest date on any Persian carpet. A dealer rebuilt it in the 1890s using pieces of its damaged twin.
artworks.lookCloser: At one end a cartouche holds a couplet by Hafiz, the words 'the work of the servant of the threshold, Maqsud Kashani', and the date 946 (1539–40). The two lamps differ in size.

artworks.title: Wilton Diptych
artworks.blurb: Richard II kneels on bare rocky ground, presented by John the Baptist and the sainted English kings Edmund and Edward the Confessor to the Virgin and Child, who stand among eleven angels in a flowering meadow. Painted for the king by an unknown French or English artist, this portable altarpiece is a rare survival of English royal panel painting, rich in lapis blue and gold.
artworks.lookCloser: The angels wear Richard's white hart badge. At the top of the banner a tiny orb shows a green island with a white tower in a silver sea: England, under Mary's protection.

artworks.title: Rucellai Madonna
artworks.blurb: The Virgin sits on a slanting wooden throne with the Christ Child, while six kneeling angels, three on each side, seem to hold the throne aloft against a gold ground. A Florentine confraternity commissioned it in 1285 from the Sienese painter Duccio for Santa Maria Novella. It is the largest surviving thirteenth-century panel painting, and for centuries it was credited to Cimabue.
artworks.lookCloser: The contract demanded costly ultramarine for Mary's robe, but conservators found cheaper azurite. The roundels on the frame show saints and Dominicans, among them Dominic and Thomas Aquinas.

artworks.title: Lion Hunt of Ashurbanipal
artworks.blurb: Carved for the North Palace at Nineveh, these reliefs show King Ashurbanipal killing lions released from cages into an arena ringed by soldiers, using arrows, spears and his sword. The king keeps a formal profile, but the lions leap, twist, collapse and die in closely observed poses. Made a generation before Nineveh fell in 612 BCE, they were probably once painted.
artworks.lookCloser: Find the attendant in a small cage on top of a crate, lifting the gate to release a lion. Elsewhere a dying lioness, pierced by arrows, drags her paralysed hind legs.

artworks.title: Victorious Youth
artworks.collection: J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles
artworks.blurb: A slim, nude young athlete raises his right hand to touch the olive wreath of victory on his head. Cast by the lost-wax method, the bronze probably stood among victor statues at a sanctuary such as Olympia. Fishermen netted it in the Adriatic off Fano in 1964; the Getty bought it in 1977, and Italy has pursued its return through the courts.
artworks.lookCloser: His nipples and lips are inlaid in copper, and his eye sockets are empty: the eyes were once inlaid, probably with bone.

artworks.title: Benin Ivory Pendant Masks
artworks.blurb: Made to be worn on a cord at the chest or hip, these small ivory masks portray Idia, the first Iyoba, or Queen Mother, of Benin and mother of Oba Esigie. The palace guild of carvers made them in the early sixteenth century for royal rites. Two near-identical examples, taken by British forces from the Oba's palace in 1897, are now in London (shown) and New York.
artworks.lookCloser: Her pupils and the scarification on her forehead are inlaid with iron. The openwork crown alternates mudfish with small bearded heads of Portuguese traders.

artworks.title: Hoa Hakananai'a
artworks.blurb: This moai, with heavy brow, long ears and jutting chin, was carved from dark lava rather than the island's usual reddish tuff. It stood half buried in a stone house at Orongo, the ceremonial village of the birdman cult, when the crew of HMS Topaz took it in 1868. Rapa Nui islanders have since asked for its return.
artworks.lookCloser: Walk round to the back: two birdmen, a sooty tern, ceremonial dance paddles and vulva symbols were carved there later. When collected, these reliefs were painted red and white.

artworks.title: Emperor Taizong Receiving the Tibetan Envoy
artworks.blurb: Emperor Taizong sits on a litter carried by palace women with fans and a canopy, while the Tibetan envoy Gar Tongtsen, a court official in red and an interpreter stand before him. The scene records the embassy of 640–41 that arranged Princess Wencheng's marriage to the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo. The composition is Yan Liben's; this scroll is probably a faithful Song copy.
artworks.lookCloser: The emperor is drawn far larger than anyone around him, a scale of rank. Collectors' seals and inscriptions show the scroll was already treasured by the early fourteenth century.

artworks.title: Great Buddha of Kamakura
artworks.blurb: This seated Amida Buddha, cast in bronze from about 1252, replaced a wooden statue damaged by a storm in 1248. Probably cast by Ōno Gorōemon or Tanji Hisatomo, it was once housed in a hall that storms wrecked twice and the tsunami of 1498 finally swept away. Since then it has sat in the open air at Kōtoku-in.
artworks.lookCloser: Traces of the original gold leaf survive near the ears. The hands rest in the lap in the gesture of meditation, and visitors can step inside the hollow body.

artworks.title: Virgin of the Rocks
artworks.medium: Oil on panel, transferred to canvas
artworks.blurb: In a dim grotto of jagged rock, Mary draws the infant John the Baptist close with one arm and holds her other hand over the Christ Child, who blesses him, while the angel Uriel looks out at us. Generally held to be the earlier of Leonardo's two versions, it probably relates to a 1483 Milan commission. Soft sfumato shadow binds figures and rocks together.
artworks.lookCloser: Uriel points at John, a gesture Leonardo dropped from the later London version. The plants at the figures' feet are painted with a botanist's care.

artworks.title: Travellers among Mountains and Streams
artworks.medium: Hanging scroll, ink and light colour on silk
artworks.blurb: A sheer central peak fills most of the silk, rising behind a foreground of boulders and scrubby trees, with a thin waterfall on its right and a band of mist between near and far. At the bottom a mule train moves along the road, tiny against the rock. Possibly Fan Kuan's only surviving work, it set the ideal of monumental landscape for centuries.
artworks.lookCloser: Fan Kuan's signature is hidden among the leaves at lower right, behind the mule train, and was only rediscovered in 1958. A temple roof shows through the trees on the cliff.

artworks.title: Wind God and Thunder God Screens
artworks.medium: Pair of two-panel folding screens, ink and colour on gold leaf on paper
artworks.blurb: On two gold screens the wind god Fūjin rushes in from the right with his bag of winds billowing overhead, and the thunder god Raijin answers from the left within his ring of drums. Between them is nothing but gold. Unsigned but firmly given to Tawaraya Sōtatsu, the screens are a National Treasure, later copied by Ogata Kōrin and Sakai Hōitsu.
artworks.lookCloser: The gods ride clouds pooled with tarashikomi, ink dropped into still-wet pigment. Both figures press against the outer edges, leaving the wide gold centre empty.
